div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.
MY DEAR NELLII,

The loveliest hats for demi-mourning wear this summer are the bergere and the plateau. The former is very simple, merely a low, round crowned affair, made of black crinoline, with a wide and slightly fluted brim trimmed with a binding of black taffetas and a wreath of black and white roses set round the crown very closely massed and quite fiat. The plateau is also flat, and is of three types; one a merely single plate raised about a half wreath of flowers or a scarf of taffetas posed upon the hair; another two discs sandwiching a closely-set wreath of blossoms; and the third a single round of straw with one end folded over. Other varities are possible, for the tilt in the case of the single round may come at the side and be trimmed underneath with a mass of flowers or a millinery bird like a pigeon, or it may be so arranged that the hat dips well over the eyes.

This year the newest and neatest skirts, both in serge and linen, are made corselet fashion, the points back and front coming some three or four inches above the waist-line,, and are well boned. Over this the soft blouse pouches prettily, and all as trim about the waist where too often an ugly iliatus occurs between skirt and waistbelt. But a -capital belt has just come out which certainly obviates such an occurrence. At the back is an ,oblong pliable piece of metal, over which is stretched the belt proper of brocaded ribbon, or a piece of lace, framed between folds of black satin, -which pass round the waist, ending in a bow with lace-inserted ends at the side. Under this is a broad band of elastic springing from the clasp behind and buckled in front, which keeps the blouse down splendidly round the waist. What- ever the belt be made of, it must be broad behind and narrow in front, to give the figure a long, straight-fronted appearance and a ahcrt bad, behind.

Dust cloaks are in great demand now that the dry weather has given place to showers. The variety of these useful garments is almost as great as that of the gowns they are intended to protect. Some are in glace silk, others in a lighter thinner silk, some in covert coating, and others, again, in alpaca, or even brown holland. In choosing one, care should be taken to select a material that is, at least, shower-proof. The alpacas and tussores are Mot so, and even a few minutes' rain reduces them to a pitiable condition. Covert coating, unlined, snakes the ideal dust cloak, when shower-proof. The covert coating is protective against dust. Ooe need not choose it in the dull and dirty-looking shades, in which it is only too often seen, for it is made in blither tones, in gray or holland colour. Ina waterproofed materials are some time very dingy, too, but they can be had in shepherd's plaid, or in a soft and pleasing shade of gray. Ic is a mistake to have a coloured cloak for wearing when driving, for when a shower follows upon clouds of dust, as it often does, the colour soon becomes streaky, and never quite recovers its first fine, care- less freshness.

Reu is undoubtedly the colour tor sunshades this season, and coarse-spotted muslin the fashion- able material, slightly fulled on to the frame ; some Ihave a lining of white muslin, which softens the glare of the red, and gives a more becoming tinge to the complexion. Rustic wooden handles are the thing, tied with a bow of ribbon or entwined with a cluster of ripe cherries and their leaves. 'or those who prefer less dazzling tones, there are charmingly simple batiste or muslin sunshades in white, pink, blue, and green, which look just the thing; chiffons and frills are out of place. The neck-bands of very thin gowns are always e unlined, unstiffened lace, unless they are entirely dispensed with and a very narrow tucker only sewn into the top of the bodice. In this case a 'velvet throatiet or a bead necklace is usually worn. INhite and cream muslin dresses are also in vogue, es are entire gown of lace made over mercerised cotton or silk. For river wear, holland and c °loured linens are being largely used, while yet another modish type of hot-weather dress is white so ohair often trimmed with strapping of black 1;1 a c . This mohair, which is really our old friend alpaca under a new name, is ideal for summer wear, except that it spoils is whetted by even the acnost transient shower. The holland frocks are trimmed with coarse lace of exactly the same hue, with an open-worked embroidery, and the linens Eire frequently ornamented in the same way, although sometimes they are trimmed with stitched bands of linen of a contrasting colour. Nearly all these dresses have deep belts of black or white glace silk. - -
Your loving Jusitra

div.head: BOWLING.
div.p: BOWLING.
Inter-County Competition-: Yorkshire Defeat Lancashire.

The annual engagement between Lancashire and York- shire was played at Mirfield on Saturday. over a green so fine in condition that bowls travelled rapidly without much effort on the part of the players. Owing to this several of the better casts were of no value to the player. As usual at these engagements, the presi ',eat and vice-president of each county led off the play. and the Lancashire men set an ex- cellent example to their followers. 's he keenest struggle of the afternoon was that between Berry. Warrington South, against Idoorhouse, of Skipton. The latter was in front up to the 21st end,when by an extra effort the lead was changed and the totals called. 15'13 in favour of Lancashire. Next a tie was declared, and Berry by some extraordinary play reached the 20th point, his opponent's score remaining stationary. Then Moorhouse brought the figures up to 2j all, and in the next end the goal was attained. Scores :

div.head: TO BEFRIEND FACTORIES.
div.p: TO BEFRIEND FACTORIES.
Against the Long-Hour System.

The Derby magistrates, we ere. have during the 'nit twelve months irtlictid exemplary fines on employers keeping girls on illegal overtime. In the course of an interview in the t• Derby Express," Mrs Marian Pipe,of 53, Upper Boundary-road, Darby, relates her early experience of workshop life, to show the evil eft, ct of long hours. " Early in life," she said, "I began to earn a living in a large workshop with other young women. In those days LONG HOURS WERE IILE RULE rather than the exception. I was too delicate for the long confinement in a room not too well veitilated, and the unhealthy life left its mark upon me even when I gave the work ,up. My health had improved by the time I married, but trlfortunat,ly I lost my husband five years ago and the shock had a serious effect. For two yea's my health went from la.ci to worse. Elmtore did not seem to understand my case, they told me I was consumptive and completely done up from nervous prostration. I was very pale and I had deep dark circles under the eyes, as if

Tea was served to him in his privacy. "There's been a lady here inquiring for you, sir," said the butler; as he set the tray on the table. "She said that she must see you very particularly, but we would not leeher in.

"Who was it? I suppose you knew her?" "Well, the footman and me, sir, thought as it might have been Misp Lane, the young lady that used to be at the post-office. But there was a child in her arms, sir, and—" "Humph! Well, you did quite right not to let her In. She went away, I suppose, without asking a lot of questions ?" "Yes, sir, only siying that she must see you, sir, some time tornight. She means to come again I think, sir." "Well, I'm not at home if she does. Let me Itmw the instant she is gone. You understand, the moment she leaves the place."

"If it weren't for-the confounded servants," he muttered to himself as the matt left the room. "They're always in the way, always prying into one's affairs, alwayta hindrancitk tut tUre seems something providential in this visit of Kitty's. If only I could smuggle her into the house unknown to the servants." Be lapsed into thought for moment and a terrible look came into his face. "Poor Kitty! She has clung very closely to me. The girl really loves me. Shall ll' " He stood in the middle of the room debating the matter in his own mind. It was some time before he came to a conclusion, and then he saw the whole course open before him. "It is my only way. There is no help for it."

The darkness grew deep before the butler at length came with the report that Miss Lane had again called and had been sent away. The moment the man had left Low donned his hat, and, slipping out at a side door, unobserved by the servants; quickly made his way down the carriage avenue that led to the main road.
He was not long in overtaking the object of his search.

"Kitty!" The woman stopped and turned. "Douglas!" "You want to see me I"' he said "Come back. I left orders that I was not to be disturbed; but I didn't know it was you." • The woman still clasped her child in her arms —she had brought it in the hope that its pleading silence might influence her husband's heart in the reconciliation she • wished to compass. She walked back to the house with him.

"What you have to say must be said without the servants knowing you have spoken with me," he, said. "Come through this door. He opened the private entrance through which he had passed in pursuit of her, and together they passed in and made their way up to the room he had left but .a minute or two before.

"Now," he said, "I'm afraid I haven't much time for words. Say what you have to say." For answer the woman, with tears in her eyes, burst into a piteous appeal. She pleaded her love for him, and his oft-expressed affection for her, and begged him to leave the place and fly with her. At first he was obdurate, playing his part well, but as she poured forth her petition, he seemingly relented and at length told her, as he took her in his arms, that he would leave with her that very night. "I have never loved any other,' Bitty," he said; "you only. We will get away from this place within an hour. The last train leaves in fifty minutes. Can you forgive me all the wrong I have done ? "

She put her arms about his neck and kissed bim. Hers was a wild, fierce passion, and, withal, a last- ing one. "We shall need refreshment before we go," 'he said. "Here, I have some wine in this cabinet. Let Ine pour you out a glass." He took-out .a &cante/. and she tool/ the Wine from his hand and drank it off. The drink seemed wiry strong, for very soon a drowsiness came over her and her head began to swim. aDonglas," she said, "I feel very strange. I have a pain in my head. I am so tired." She leant back in the chair, and her • eyes closed heavily. Low took the infant in his arms. "This will be a trifle more difficult," said he, "but---" ; There was a great noise at the door downstairs. Low paused with the child upraised. The clamour was renewed. There 'were the voices of servants, and tones that he cotild have sworn were those of old Pryke, and another strangely familiar voice which, try .as he plight, he could not quite individualise. , "We must see him. And now." There was no mistake about that voice. It was the guttural topes of Perkins, the village policeman. Some z develop- ment had arisen. Low did not mistake the mean- ing of the visit. These men had come to arrest him.
CHAPTiR
"IN TUN RAMC OF TUi LAW."

The parley only lasted a moment more. Dis- regerding the butler and footmen who averred that their master was out, the men pushed by these dignitaries in the hail, and commenced to ascend the stairs. As they did 40, Low quietly closed his door, which he had partially opened to listen, and turned the key. He heard tha men searching the various rooms for him. At length they came to his room and tried the door. , , "Open in the name of the law," shouted Perkins, but Low kept perfectly still. "I don't believe there's anyone in there," spoke the constable's voice. "It's only a small room by the look of it. Let's search that bedroom over there again." But the strangely familiar voice 'broke in. "No, no. This is his favourite resort. Demand entrance once more, and if that doesn't do burst the door . open." Again was Low called upon to open, and still he maintained his silence. Suddenly Kitty's child raised its voice in one piteous cry. It was enough for theinen outside. Upon the lock fell' the heavy blows of sticks, and the utmost force was exerted to burst opetf the door. At last the hinges creaked, the lock bufst, and the way was clear. Low stood in the Middle of the room. He had searched the place in vain forarevolver, but when be had found one, diseevered that he had left all his cartridges downstairs. In. default he had seized the poker, and stood prepared to defend his liberty, and, if possible, to make a dash for it. But at the sight that met his eyes the poker dropped from his hands and he reeled back in horror. For the first man to enter the room was his cousin, Martin Fenwick, the convict reported dead at Smilehurst, and whose funeral Low had attended—no ghostly visitant, but Martin Fenwick, in flesh and blood, grey haired and aged, perhaps, yet the true Martin Fenwick, alive and well, the lawful master of Fenwick Chase and affianced lover of Grace 'Tendon. _

----- With n gasp he fell back from before his cousin, making no attempt at defence, and in a trice the otHers were upon him, and he was a prisoner. "I arrest you for the murder of Squire Fenwick and Harold Manton," said the constable.

Low made an effort to recover himself. He stammered out his innocence and his absolute ignorance of any such individual as Harold Manton, but little heed was taken of his words, for the men had fourd. Kitty lying prostrate in the chair and the child by her side, crying lustily, and were doing what they could to restore consciousness to the one and hush the cries of the other. The servants had crowded frightened around the door.
"Take this woman to one of the bedrooms," said "artin, "and send for the nearest actor."

-'orders were obeyed with alacrity. Inetinc- widaV the servants recognised his tone of authority and hurried to do his bidding. "And now, constable," said he, "I am at your service. lam free to be arrested as a convict at large. Do your duty. I have had freedom long enough to attain the ends at which I aimed. I can well afford to suffer imprisonment a little longer." He looked at Low, who had never taken his eyes off his cousin.
"Not dead! Not dead!" gasped Low. His eyes expressed the wonder he felt, and Martin answered it.

"Still alive," he said. "No thanks to.you. You thought you had done for me when you fired that dastardly shot at Bernard Bay." Low started, but recovered himself. "I don't know what you are talking about," he said. "Then I will make it more clear to you. You remember firing at me twice as I ran through the forest. You remember tracking me through the tangle of trees to the open country. You remember the shepherd's hut on the hill, and meeting a pikel coming down the bridle path. 'But you little know that the man you pursued on the further side of the hill was not worth a single shot to you. Neither do you know that the man whose, life you coveted was the yokel who doubled on y-ig and saw , you shoot 1t:. friend in the back, saw hi-s reel and fall into the water, saw you throw your revolver out into the tide as you heard footsteps approach- 4sg and followed you as you ran off across the

div.head: LADDER OF GUILT.
div.p: THE LADDER OF GUILT.
(Capyrzgit.)
Ey ULYSS . ROGERS, Author of "For Love and the Queen," "Wedded
in Mystery," &e-.
0-HAI'TER XXXVL
A PUZZLING SITUATION.
The tew-corner, as the crowd standing open- mouthed with astonishment instantly recognised, was Kitty Lane, recently assistant-postmistress at Fenwick. •

"You—you lie, woman!' shouted Low, recovet- ing his self-possession -by a palpable effort. don't know you. What mid freak is this ? Come, Grace, enter the carriage, and we'll get away from these brawlers."

But Grace hesitated. She conk] scarcely believe that her ears had heard aright. The charges that had been made were monstrous. It was impossible that they could be true. And yek deep within her heart, she mistrusted Douglas. Kitty, clasping her child close to her bosom, seeing Grace halt, darted in between her and Low.

"You coward! You who married me two years ago, who kept me out of sight in London, nOt because I should disgrace yon, as I once thought, but because of what has happened to-day! I might have suspected, I. ought to have suspected. And then to try and get me out of the country--" "The woman is raving mad," shouted Low, appealing to the constable. "No," she replied. "I have just returned to my senses. I was mad when I was deluded by your promises into robbing Miss Hendon of her letter; mad when I married you in the nettle of Bowden, which you falsely adopted; mad when I per- mitted myself to be sent to Liverpool two days ago; mad to believe that you would sell your estate and follow me to America. I have been mad, mad all the time, and only now have I returned to my 'senses. This marriage to-day is illegal. I call upon everybody to witness that I am Douglas Low's wife. I can prove it." i She spoke n high tones, but there was the force- ful element of truth in her voice, and her state- ment did not fall on altogether unbelieving ears. "I leave her in your hands, constable," said Low. "Poor creature! She is quite demented. Come, Grace. What, you refuse?" "I do!" she said. "You must disprove what this woman says. It is a grave charge.' "But she is a mad woman. That is apparent on the face of it.

"I am no mad woman," interrupted Kitty. "I can prove every word I say if I am but given • day or two to get my box from Liverpool. I had no time to bring it with me. I saw the announce- ment of the wedding in a Sunday paper just before my boat sailed and caught the next train .to stop it." To add to the confusion old Jezebel Parr, who by this time had forced herself through the crowd, in high tones 'recommenced her menaces, and the onlookers, grasping slowly the situation, stood open-mouthed, anxious to miss nothing of so relishing a situation. "It is an indignity, an outrage!" cried Low, appealing to the police-officer, who was vainly trying to keep people back and at the same time satisfy his own curiosity by catching as much of , the women's stories as he could. 'Grace, once more, are you coining with me? You are my wife." Grace stood nerveless, white. The ordinary excitement of a wedding morning had been ten times intensified by the scene outside the church. "I cannot," she said. "I will go back 'with Mr. Robins. When this is all disproved—" "Please yourself," he interrupted. "Let me' help you." He handed her into the carriage. "You will come with me ? " she said to Kitty. "I want to talk to you." _

The woman stepped in, and Mr. Robins followed with Mrs. Robins. They drove back to the schoolhouse, whilst Low leaped into the next carriage, and,with the wild ravings of Jeiebel Parr still ringing in his ears, drove off to the Chase. - The crowd still loitered about the church, excitedly discussing the extraordinary things of which they had been witnesses. Not one believed the improbable story of old Jezebel Parr. "But that 'ere Lane gal's yarn, that's soineut wot beats me," said a bystander. "I said there was someul atween the young squire and 'er two years ago, and I zed zo at the time down in the tap of the Cock and Whistle." "Aye, aye, so you did—so you did," replied Rayner, the smith; "and my son seed the squire. and the gal off by the train to Lunnon. It's a queer ending to a wedding, anyhow." The constable was the most puzzled of all. In the whole of his career he had never' been called upon to deal with such a case. If either woman'is. story was correct it was his blisinese.to arrest the young squire, an act of sacrilege which he could not bring himself to commit. A wrongful arrest of the young squire would mean the blasting of his career in the county constabulary and make his life in Fenwick excessively uncomfortable. He knew the nature of Mr. Low too well, he soliloquised. On the other hand, had he not neglected his duty in failing to arrest both Jezebel Parr and the woman who claimed to be the squire's wife, for causing a disturbance? Having at length chased the crowd from the church gates he went home to dinner, with his mind in a hopeless quandary.

div.head: CHAPTER XXXVII.
div.p: CHAPTER XXXVII.

ONE LAST ACT OF TREACHERY. Low reached the Chase in a chafing passion. For the old hag, Parr, he cared not a snap of his finger. He could dare her to do her worst; but the sudden appearance of Kitty had upset every plan he had made. Her accusation was true, and it was serious. Two years jbefore he had s•eretly married her in London m order to keep her quiet when she had threatened to ease her conl science of the postal robbery and to bring an action for breach of promise of marriage against him, a confession and an action which would have ruined all his plans. Yet he had made his arrangements to work to a nicety. His last hurried run to London was to see her off to Liverpool en route for New York, where he had promised to meet her after disposing of the estates. He had given her a note of intro- duction to fictitious people in Maryport, and intended running over, as soon as he was com- fortably settled at the Chase with Grace, to work Kitty's final ruin in the States.

What meddling paper had inserted the announce- ment of his wedding that caught her eye at the last moment and brought her back again? He had no doubt the paragraph was inspired by Henderson, the local postmaster, who acted as district correspondent for several newspapers. He cursed himself that he had forgotten the danger of the press. Half a sovereign would have kept Hender- son from making the thing public. Just that one minute flaw and the whole fabric of his designs had come tottering to the ground. What a fogl he had been!

He snapped out a harsh "No," to the request of the surprised butler whether he would take any lunch, and buried himself in his private room thinking out the best course of action to be pursued. It was fortunate that he could rely on Perkins's thick head. A smart constable anxious to dis- tinguish himself might have arrested him already upon the charges that had been made. Perkins would require a night to sleep it over, and very definite orders into the bargain, before he ventured upen such an enterprise. There was but one course open—to make a bolt. The case against him was clear enough. Although he had married Kitty under a false name, that did not make the marriage invalid.. He reviewed the ladder of guilt down which he had climbed, and, as is the custom with morally weak and diseased natures, put the blame upon circumstance rather than upon himself. If Martin Fenwick had not crossed his path at the first, he would have been as guiltless as the most righteous man in the country. Some blind fate had worked persistently and consistently against him, or.why should he who, as a boy, loathed crime, have been plunged into the depths in which he had Wallowed? He remembered how he had fought out the battle on the Downs on that fatal night before his soul had been steeped in the blood of his cousin, and a wave of true repentance passed over him. But it was only momentary. The thought that now, at last, after he had risked so much, after he had sunk character and honour and all that men hold dear to win Grace Hendon he was further , from winning her than ever, tore him with a mad anguish. He was an Ishmael with his hand againstagainst Thema devil withinn'sehandand every man's hand him, chained for one brief moment, was loose again. It would be useless to do anything other than; remain in the house until nightfall. Then the first thing to be considered was his personal safety. He gave instructions that on no pretence was any- one to be admitted to the house, and remained

sands to the westward and disappeared in the brush. wood beyond." "If your game is to try and connect me with the death of the man who escaped from Smilehurst, you have a difficult thing on hand. I have an alibi." "And I have your revolver which I searched for when the tide went down, and your handkerchief which a briar snatched from your pocket as you hurried from the bay into the brushwood. It has your name in full, and your initials are on the stock of the weapon. But that crime is but the outcome of a former one. I had not thought that my innocence was to be proved at the expense of your guilt, but it is quite certain that it will be. My chance came when I was thought dead. As a ' dead' man, I could work in my own interest. I revealed myself to nobody, wrote to nobody, but worked to collect proofs. These I now have, and I live once more " The constable turned his back for a moment, and on the instant Low darted out of the door and made for the staircase. In a moment Perkins, Pryke, Martin and a servant were in full pursuit. Taking the stairs half-a-dozen at a time Low reached the bottom before the others had gained the top. The hall door was standing open, but at the entrance stood Jezebel Parr, gossiping with some of the servants. They turned as the noise of the rush reached their ears. The constable was shouting to them to cut off the retreat. It would be risky to try and pass them. Quickly the hunted man turned into one of the rooms leading off the hall, a room in which he usually kept his gun and his sporting accoutre- ments. Banging the door behind him he turned I the key. "Quick, to the back of the house. You can get in by the window," cried Martin, and, obeying his word, they darted in the direction he indicated. The window was reached, but it was high from the ground and firmly closed. They could see into the room, however, and as they hesitated a moment before smashing the glass, they saw Low reach to a drawer and take out something which he held in his hand. The next instant he had lifted his hand to his head ; there was a loud report and Douglas Low fell forward heavily to the floor. He was still living when they reached him, though the ugly wound in his forehead from which the blood flowed in a thick stream told how useless was all earthly aid. They lifted him carefully and bore him to the couch. The end was not protracted, but the moments that intervened gave Low his one chance of peni- tence. He availed himself of a few seconds' consciousness to inake a dying confession, and Lawyer Pryke was lot slow to take down the particulars. Slowly and with feeble breath the dying man told how he murdered Squire Fenwick in mistake for his cousin, against whom he had aimed his gun, told of the fire at Farmer Hendon's, and lastly of the chase from Smilehurst and of the shooting of the convict in the boat. With his last remaining strength he scrawled his name at the foot of the sheet Mr. Pryke presented before him, and murmuring: "Forgive me, Martin, old fellow; God forgive me," his eyes darkened and his soul went out. It was a terrible end, yet how just a retribution that the hand which had brought death to others should at length turn on its owner and speed the grim messenger to him. The doctor had arrived. He looked at Low, felt his pulse, and shook his head. "I couldn't have saved him; nothing could. Where is the woman?" They took him upstairs. Kitty still lay uncon- scious, but a glance at her face gave him hope. He repeated the operation of feeling the pulse, I inquired if emetics had been given, and listened to her faint breathing. I Then with a smile: "You have acted quite right," he said. "The antidote was given just in time. We shall save her."

div.head: CHAPTER XXXIX.
div.p: CHAPTER XXXIX.
AT LAST.

Outside Fenwick churchyard lies a rough patch of unconsecrated ground, and there is one mound there, a mound always distinguishable among the long grass and weeds by a single wreath, ever fresh and green. The grave has but one solitary visitor --a woman; but she is constant week after week, year in and year out, and never comes but she bedews the mound, though it be the last resting- place of a slayer of his fellow-men and of himself, with hot tears of genuine grief. Truly the love of a woman is a mystery surpass- ing the wisdom of man. Inside the consecrated area is another grave which few would miss. For the monument at its head can be seen far down the road, and there are few in the village but can recite the story of the young squire's friendship for Harold Manton. It is a cherished record of the way in which Manton, drafted to Smilehurst at the same time as Martin, and discharged from prison three months afterwards, arranged to wait off Bernard with a small sailing boat and a punt for the: first night that would give his friend the chance of escape; and how the late wrongful squire shot Manton in mistake for his cousin and wounded hi in so badly that he fell into the water and was drowned. All this story and that of the Fenwick mystery the village have by heart, and it needs little encouragement to urge them to tell the local romance from the very beginning down to the time when the present squire, having escaped prison, discovered that the missing bullet which had passed through the old squire when he was shot, was in the possession of Jezebel Parr, who had quietly abstracted it from beneath the rowlock of the punt, and had also found and appropriated the bird which Martin had shot but a moment before the great tragedy. With her inborn cunning Jezebel had extracted the shot from the bird and had kept it, a powerful witness to prove that the man who had fired the one was not likely to have fired the oth4 a moment afterwards.

Moreover, as Martin had discovered, the bullet which took old Squire Fenwick's life was of a kind recently patented, and an affidavit from the makers proved Douglas Low to have received the first consignment ever despatched to that county, only the day before the tragedy. These proofs, added to detailed circumstance and Low's confession, cleared the stain from 15fartin's name for ever.

Prosperous times have fallen upon Fenwick of late years, and the bright-faced, grey-headed young squire is the most popular man in the county. ile finds an unceasing pleasure in making easier the hard paths of his tenants, and with a touching gratitude almost reverences minute life, for the very sight of an animal of the lower order brings to mind his friend Manton's pet and tha scene which first endeared him to the man who was to sacrifice his life for him.

Sometimes, however, a great sadness will over- cast Martin's features, and as evening draws in he will become silent and abstracted and moody. Then it is that a light hand will touch him on the shoulder, and he will turn to look into the sweetest, dearest eyes he ever beheld, whilst a .soft, low voice says: . .

"Come, dearest, it is all over now. Forget it. my love. Listen, little Grace and Martin an calling for you. It is the children's hour. It's impossible to get them to bed till they have had their usual romp." Then does Martin Fenwick thank God for his great happiness, and hissing his wife hurries off to fulfil his nightly programme. A few minutes later the entry into the nursery of a frolicsome but very human-looking rhinoceros, who, on all fours, undergoes a frantic hunt, and suffers crick in the back and skinned knee joints, counting them joys, is the signal for boisterous yells of merriment which fill the old Chase with the most delightful . music Martin and Grace Fentdick have ever heard.

div.head: PRIZE DAY AT WARRINGTON TRAINING COLLEGE.
div.p: PRIZE DAY AT WARRINGTON TRAINING COLLEGE.
Speech by the Bishop of Chester.

The annual distribution of prizes to the students at the Warrington Training College took plice oo Satur- day. The Right Rev the Lord Bishop of Chester pre- sided, and WRS supported on the platform by the follow- ing members of the College Committee :—The Dean of Manchester (the Rev Canon Maclure), the Reverend Canons Gore, Holme, Penrhyn, Stanoing, the 11,-v T K Dickson, and Messrs H B Gilmour, El R Jovnson, J Kendall, H Radcliffe, Dr Watkins, and Mr H S Wood- ccck. Letters of apology for absence were received from the Lord Bishop of Liveroool,Archdeacon Fletcher, and Canons Feilden and Nunn.

div.head: SPEECH BY THE PRINCIPAL.
div.p: SPEECH BY THE PRINCIPAL.

The PRINCIPAL (the Rev Morley Sce—s:e-nson, said, he could not toe k upon the students behind him witbout remembering that they were the last who would wear the title of quepn's scholars. Whether they were at the present moment queen's scholars or king's scholars he was not sure, but this he knew : that when they entered the college they were all queen's scholars, and he was quite sure they would understand what was in his mina without his saying more. All their lives the students would feel proud of the honour and privilege of having borne the title of queen's scholars. When they knew that the example set by.their late beloved Queen was in the purity and holiness of her own life, the syerms,thy and affection she showed to others and the wonderful influence she exercised upon all, perhaps teachers, more than any other class of the community, would fed that such an example was one which they could set before them as an ideal throughout the whole of their lives. (Applause.) The Principal proceeded to refer to the lamented death of Sir John Stainer, the musical examiner of the college. They had passed through the regular cycle of examination, and passed through them with success, with lists upon which they might lock with pride. (Ha r, hear.) In every subject in which they had been examined during the year they could show a result which was distinctly creditable. (Applause.) They had been crowned during the last few days by the result of an examination in a subject which in that college was of the greatest importance of any, the sub'eect of religious knowledge, a result which had caused them much thankfulness. The major part by far of the students bad been placed in the first class, the minor part in the second, and none in the third. (Applause.) Passing from that joyful topie, outside the college in the rest of the eoucational world the present was a very stormy period. What:with education tills being intro- duced and education bills being withdrawn, what with , Cockerton judgments, and what with certain classes to be discontinued and certain teachers to lose their occupa- tions, they all felt there was a sense of turmoil and unrest in the educational world which must be very des- tmsing. What a blessing it was to turn from that very turbulent state of things in the outside world to the extremely peaceful state of things in the training colleges, They were of the educational world, but went on with their work qnite undisturbed by all these exist- ing things outside. They had simply to train teachers, and whatever education bills were introduced or with- drawn, and whatever judgments might be delivered by those in high places, he tcok it that one thing was cer tam, there would always be a need for teachers. (Hear- , hear). So they went on with their quiet work indepen, dent of these turmeils, educating and training ths teachers of the future, and doing, he hoped, a work which wae for the erod of the country. (Applause). Put it must not be thought that they never had anything to rails the cairn ot the training colleges. In future there wauld be no examination at the end of the nrst year That, of course, must be a very serious cause of ' grief. (Laughter.) Following upon that they had received only in the last few days a very important cir- cular from the Board of Education, which bad almost completely at the stroke of the pen revolution:zed the syllabus upon which they worked. In future there would be no syllabus. They were to go as they pleased. They were, subject to taking certain hues of education. to draw up their own syllabus, they were to manage and conduct in any way they thought fit their own examinatioes, and generally they were given a very free hand indeed. He did not know quite what to say upon this. It was very difficult to speak of a revolution while the revolulion was going on, and judge it as calmly as might be done many years after it bad happened. The trend of thought In the present day was rather to swing the- pendulum to the other extreme. Instead of a possible. overenued of examnation they were to have hardls any at all. Examinations were being discontinued in the primary schools, and it looked very mocla as though they would be discontinued in the training colleges. Whether that would make for good or not he thought it , was too early to say. He declined to express a positive opinion, but he hoped the training colleges would rise to the situation and would devote themselves to producing be the useful line of work they laid down, good teachers in the future. (Applause.) Rsferring to the presence of the Bishop of Chester, Mr Btevenson spoke ot the great ar d real interest be had always taken in the college, and said they were deeply grateful to him for that interest. He might remind the Bishop that it was eleven years since he bad presided at a similar gather- ing there. On that eccasion he gave thsm a maxim. He was speaking at the advantages of the teaching of cookery, and summed up his advice to the girls, having regard to their possible future relations with the other sex, in the epigraniatic and terse maxim " Feed ths brute." (Laughter.) That maxim had never been for- gotten. It produced an impression which remained to the present day. (Laughter)

div.head: SPEECH BY THE BISHOP OF CHESTER.
div.p: SPEECH BY THE BISHOP OF CHESTER.

The BISHOP OF CHESTER said he wished in the first place to disabuse their minds of the ides that hi was a rurininer of other people's good things. He could only po that eleven yews ago, on an occasion tho details ot which he had forgotten, he did not pretend to his audience that be invented that very happy maxim re- ferred to by the Principal. He simply passed on what had become a classic in the proverbial philosophy of England and ad English-speaking races. (Laughter). Ho would not dwell further upon the matter, but would ask them to believe that ha did not eleven years ago pose as having created what he simply appropriated for their tenefit. (Laugkit r). His main proceeding would be to bring before them and offer a few comments upon the report of his Majesty's Inspector of Training Colleges, Mr Scott Coward who ur fortunately was ill and unable to be with the council of the college to give them the bent fit of his very suggestive comments and notes viva voce. First of all, under the head of reading and recit- ation, he said, " These important branches of the stu- dents' instruction are being systematically, carefully and very successfully attended to," and in particular he menti,.ned voice production. They would all feel that ice production. whether they were speaking of read- ing or singing, was the very root of the matter, ond he did not 'hink it was possible to over estimate the value of sound voice production in their training colleges. It was the very foundation of beautiful singing or epeak- iog. Coming to teaching, the report read: "The leksona were AS usual, admirable in their aim, illustration and facility of delivery. They were honest, practical effort to teach." The report also referred to practice in schools. He noticed this, because he would have it understood, and he was sure the Council would wish it to be tioderstood,that those having the leadership of the college were constantly open to improvement of methods rhe report read at another point " The discipline is admirably maintained and the best spirit prevails amongst the students and staff. All work under the Principal's most wise administration in complete har- mony. The health of the students seems good in spite of the hard work, and everything Is done by means of good and most comfortable housing to mair.tain it." That was comforting news, though it was very familiar news to those interested in the college. The In.peetor went on to say " The Principal and his staff deserved every praise and the confidence of the committee for the way in which their difficult and arduous task is per- formed " Then again, "Your college is doing a most valuable work for the ceuntry in one of Is most important needs." That was what could most certainly be claimed for the training colleges. They were doing • great national and patriotic work, and th) money given to them from the central treasury was admirably expended from a national point of view. (Applause ) They might sometimes have heard comparsiona drawn between their residential training colleges and the nen-residental system. But while they fully recogn'vd the advantages of both they could not help feeling that the residential system had peculiar merits which the nation to say nothing of the church, could not afford to part with. (Applause.) In the first place here was the opportunity for cultivating a corperate spirit. They all recognised the vain' of that among men. Why not among women also? Why not so in their training colleges, where they bad all the influences which made for culture and refinement ? Where the students were scattered in lodgings outside a great deal could be done for them, and they might do a great deal for themselves, but in a re:idential college where the students were together in one institution for two or three years, they had resources and influences which were so very advantageous in the development

of the character of the students that they could no afford to part with the tvstem. (Applause.) Mese queen's scholars were going forth to take a share in tbe one great pastoral office of the church. All would bop! that they would give the best powers of their hearts Oa minds and bodies to the service of the State and tne service of Christ's Church,as having a vital share in tbe one broad manifold work of shepherding Christ's little ones. (Applause.) The Bishop then distributed tbe prizes. TIH following is the prize list : FIRST TEAR STUDENTS. Holy Scriptnre.—Rose Kennerley and Mary Martin. Holy Bible. A Warrington Boy's Miraculous Escape. Walking Day Incident. On Friday evening an alarming accident befel- little boy named Willie Jones, eight years of age' who resides with his parents at 12, Nicholsol?' street. It appears that the boy, with bl parents, went with the trip organized by the VirelP Calvinistic Church, Crostield-street, to SouthporC: and it was on the return journey that the acciden° tcok place. When near Farnworth signal box, the boy walked across the carriage, and began to Pig with the handle of the door. Without a momenu; warning, the door opened, and the boy was preciP,': toted from the train (which was going at a fa' speed),into the six-foot. Naturally the parents were horrified, and to acid to their distress, the 10 20 00; press from Warrinwton to Liverpool dashed up an,' passed the train. It was then believed by the clle- tracted parents that the boy had been cut to piece' and only after a terrific struggle was the fathe' prevented from throwing himself out, the mother_ having fainted meanwhile. During the struggle 3f.1 Jones's hand was severely crashed in the door, awl he also sustained injuries to his fingers. The CO' munication cord was pulltd without effect. however, transpired that the signalman near signal box, hearing the child's cry,got out and taking the child to the box, dressed his wounds. P.; then stopped the eleven o'clock slow train fr°,7o Liverpool, and the lad was placed in the care of tP., guard. On the arrival of the train at WarringtoPe, he was handed to his father and mother, who vg/0 naturally overwhelmed with joy at his rescue. div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
A Three Hours' Meeting.

At the Town Hall, Warrington, on Tuesday evening, the ordinary monthly meeting of the Warrington Town Council was held and the proceedings lasted nearly three hours. The Mayor (Alderman Roberts) pre- sided and there were also present :—Aldermen Fair- dough, (deputy mayor), Mocks, Bolton. Heaton, Hutchinson, Francomb, Councillors Flumpton, Smethurst, John Evans, Duncan William Pierpoint, Tinsion, Bennett, 9 Davies A J-Jolley, Greening. Sam- son, Bennett, Allison, William Roberts, A Jolley, Peacock, Forshaw, James Evans, John Roberts, Burton, Hulse, with Messrs J Lyon Whittle (town clerk), S Wilson (deputy town clerk), J Fairhurst, (borough treasurer), J Deas, (sanitary and water engineer), W S Haddock (gas engineer), W Grimsdale (electrical engineer). - -
The Magistrates' Clerk.

The MAYOR mentioned the cebject of the resignation of the Magistrates' Clerk auu we appointment of his successor. It was he said, only fair that he should put before the Council in some detail the proceedings of the magistrates' meeting held on June 25:h. The letter of resignation from Mr El B White having been read, considerable discussiort followed, and then the follow- ing resolutions were unanimously adopted.—" That the resignation of Mr El B White of the office of magis- trates' clerk be accepted"; " That subject to the approval of the Council the salary of the magistrates' clerk be continued at £5OO per annum"; and "That Mr George Freeman White be appointed magistrates' clerk for this borough." lie begged to move that the pro- ceedings of the magistrates he approved so far as the same required the approval of the Council, Alderman HEATON seconded, and it was carried. Watch Committee. Another Out Police Station.
At a meeting of the Watch Committee, held on the 13th June it was resolved "That the Chief Constable be authorised to rent 289, Winwick-road, for use as an out-station." _ .
The minutes were approved on the m3tion of the Mayor, seconded by the Deputy Mayor.
Committees :and Over-expenditure. The Old Warps Estate.

At a meeting of. the Finance Committee, held on the 10th June, it was resolved "That the security required by the Board of Guardians for the due performance of the duties of assistant overseer be affected through a guarantee society," and "That the Borough Treasurer be requested to call the attention of this committee to any proposed expenditure in excess of any committee's estimates, or in case there be no meeting of this com mittee before the Council meeting that he call the atten- tion of the Chairman or Deputy Chairman of this committee to such expenditure." It was decided that the land tax on certain premises be red e-med for the sums agreed upon with the committees, .nd as set out in the agenda. The DEPUTY MAYOR proposed the adoption of the minutes. Alderman Elmicrox seconded. Councillor SMETHURST asked whether the Finance Committee could veto whatever proceedings of any committee they thought fit. The Mason said that was not so. The resolution was simply an instruction to the Borough Treasurer to call attention to any excess so that the Finance Committee could call the attention of the particular committee to the fact and give the committee an opportunity of explaining the reason. , Alderman Bovrox thought this should be the Borough Treasurer's duty apart from any special instruction. It was part of the duty of the Finance Committee to see to these things. Councillor ELLIsox said be saw they were about to let the Old Warps estate. Be moved as an amendment to:the minntee that the strip of land fronting Knutsford- road from the Lodge to Black Bear Bridge be not included. Be thought some trees should be planted along the frost. Councillor tMETHURST seconded. He would he said, like to know whether the Council had in this connection borrowed money in such a way as would prevent them subletting any of the land for building purposes. If that was so, it was a great mistake indeed. Alderman BOLTON said the Town Hall, Park and Baths Committee had no money to spend for the purpose of planting trees. Councillor PLIMPTON said he voted for the purchase of this land on thedistinct understanding that the land would be let for building purposes. The MAYOR You were never told that; you were told that it was one of the possibilities. Councillor PLIMPTON I think I have been told It.

The ?dawn : Not in this Council Chamber. Councillor PLIMPTON : I would rot have voted for the purchase it I bad known that this was going to be a wh;te elephant. Alderman Monts said that if tnis amendment was carried it would placP/the Finance Committee in a rather awkward position. He could not say from memory how much land it involved, but it might just make the difference between the committee getting a satisfactory tender for thP plot as a whole or no tender at all. Councillor TINNION asked bow much land the amend- ment covered ? The TOWN CLERK said an arrangement could be made for the planting of trees although the land was let. Answering Councillor Tinnion he said be believed there were between four and five acres. Councillor PIERPOINT said that unless th?y could let the land, and have it cultivated in a proper manner, they would have it in a most disreputable condidon If I the committee took this strip of land and tried to culti- vate it they would find its rather serious charge. He agreed with the Town Clerk that arrangements might be made with the incoming tenant to plant trees. Alderman SEATON suggested that if they were ever likely to want the land it should be let with that reser- vation. The aleyon thought that the best suggestion. If the matter were left in the bands of the committee with that expression of opinion they would take care to re- serve the right of appropriating the land whenever they required it, Councillor ELLisex : That will meet my requirements.

_ Councillor SMETHURST asked whether ihey. were pre- vented from using the land for building purposes. Th MAYOR said it was not quite easy to answer that question definitely. straight way. They borrowed the money under an application mode to the Local Govern- ment Board, and if they wanted to re-sell any portion for building purposes they would have to re-apply to the Local Government Board for permission to do so. They were not shut out for ever from doing so. The minutes were approved. The Feathers Hotel. Sale of Surplus Land.

1 The Street Improvement and Lighting Committee at a meeting held an the 13th June' agreed to the following resolution :—" ihat the surplus land In Bridge-street and Friars' Gate and the proposed Feathers Hotel be i sold to Mr Howard Russell for the sum of £10,000." _ ... .
COUSCiIIOr BAIRD moved, and Councillor JAMES EVANS seconded, the confirmation of the minutes, which was agreed to.

Deputations. The "Picnic "to the "Clio." Lively Discussion. At a meeting of the School Attendance Committee it was reported that the average attendance at the Public Elementary Schools during the month of May was .11 8, ; it et cri on ardri rss etprsoi! onal industrial eti nrdagi npthatienr tot 3sd eh map setcmyi beo ea err anl .00ft , h9t ,h 3 el e 8 hmt cm; uei tal ytseet; that the Chairman or Deputy-Chairman and Councillor; Davies and Malkin be appointed to visit the Deaf and Dumb School and liensbaw's Blind Asylum, Blanchester; and that the Deputy-Chairman and Councillors Brough and Sampson be appointed to visit the Boys' Refuge, Liverpool, and the Truant School Hightown, in July' Councillor Eursox moved, and Councillor Duscarr seconded, the passing of the minutes. Councillor JANIES Elam said some time ago, a resolu- tion was passed by the Council that no deputation should be increased to more than three persons, and therefore he could not see why the whole of the School Attendance Ccmmittee should pay a visit to the Clio, when two members with the chairman or deputy chair- man were considered sufficient to visit the Deaf and Dumb School, Blind Asylum, and the Truant School. He had heard it said that the proposed visit was only "the picnic day of the committee," but that was not quite good enough alter the passing of the resolution to which be had already referred. It was not good enough to have that picnic at the expense of the rate- payers unless they said so. It should notgoout that it was a deputation when it was really a picnic, when it was a day's out for the committee. (Laughter.) There had been no clamour on the part of the members to go to the deaf and dumb school. the blind asylum, or the truant school. (Laughter.) Neither had there been any question as to whether three memb?rs were sufficient to form the deputation. (Renewed laughter.) He moved therefore, that the minutes pass with the exce.p two of the oue relating to the proposed visit to the Cho. Councillor A J JoLLEY seconded• Alderman BOLTON thought chat if the committee were of opinion that the whole of the members should visit the Clio they should do so. They had gone so often that it would be a mistake to stop them now. The committee worked so very 'hard that they deserved a holiday. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Ebtisms observed that the resolution of the Council to which Councillo't James Evans had referred did not effect the visits to the Clio. There was an un- derstanding by the Council that the reColution should not affect the School Attendance Committee. ' Councillor GREENING supported tbe amendment. It was not, be said, good enough for the whole of the Committee to go to the Clio at the expense of the rate- payers. The rates of the i••orough were high, and the Corp:ration ought, therefore, to be economical. There was no good purpose served by sending the whole of the

members to the Clio. He (the speaker) moved the resolution which was passed by the Council, and to which One or two members had referred, but nothing was said about the visit to the Clio by members of the School Attendance Committee. Alderman HEATON hoped the Council would not obj..ct to the whole ot the committee going to the Clio. He nad been a member of the committee for many years, and it was the only opportunity they bad of looking after the interests of the poor cuildren for whom they were responsible.

Councillor JAMES EvANs, who rose with the pqrmis sion of the Mayor to make an explanation, said he voted for the special resolution, but he had not the slightest recollection that an exemption was made in the case of the School Committee. He had no recollection even that the matter was even referred to. If memb-±rs of the committees had been going wrong so long it was no-- The MAYOR. You are trespassing beyond the explana- tion you rose to make. Councillor JAMES EvANS admitted that perhaps he Wag doing so, but he saw no reason wby the co.nmitue ahould continue to do wrong. Cu.lncillor A J JOLLEY said he quite admitted that it was important Lhat the committee should be in touch with what was going on on the Clio, but it was not I necessary that the whole of the members should go to I enable them to be in touch with the ship. No one knew better than Mclennan Heaton the abaolote necessity of regularly Visiting the institutions to which they sent children, but he strongly objected to the whole of the committee going, and simply as a picnic. Councillor WILLIAM ROBERTS did not think the money Spent on the committee was wasted. He was not a member of the School Committee, and he therefore felt all the freer to speak about the question. He had the pleasure of accompanying the members on their visit to the Clio last year, and he did not hesitate to say that he derived infairmation from that visit which, to his , mind at any rate, was exceedingly valuable, and valu- able also to every member of the committee. If the visit to the Clio was the means of inducing the coin• mitten and the magistrates to send more boys to the ship for their training, he contended that the money was thoroughly well spent. (Hear, hear ) Councillor TINNION would not like to see any resolu- tion passed which would prevent any:portion of the committse visiting the Clio. The amendment,therefore, should be altered.

Councillor JAMES EVANS wrs willing to alter his amendment to read that only three members should visit the ship. Councillor PLuareroir informed the Council that he learnt quite as much on his first visit to the Clio as be would be able to learn if ho went twenty times to it. It was,therefore, a very good suggestion that only three should be sent to the ship. He would not send the same members every year; they should go in turns. (Bear, hear.) . . . .

Councillor PIERPOINT asked what was the annual cost of the visit to the training ship. The MAYOR observed that the oast last year but one was £l4 10s. This year's figures bad not yet been published. Councillor PEACOCK: For about thirteen membns? The Maxon said there was one side of the question to be considered, and it was this—whether it was not desirable that the institutions with which they were associated, and to which they contributed something, should not be personally visited by every member of the School Committee every year at least. At the same time he contended that it would have been consistent on their part to have sent the whole of the corn mittee to the several institutions which had been named. There were circumstances connected with these establishments which rendered it extremely desirable that they should be visited and inspected in the interests of the lads from the different localities. If it happened that one of these places that had to be visited was beautifully situated it was an incident that was agreeable, but if the committee went as a body to the Clio, they should go as a body to other institutions. (Hear, hear.) The amendment was then put to the meeting andiost. It was that only three members of the committee and an offiCial should pay a visit to the Clio. The minutes were then passed.

div.head: Baths Extensions.
div.p: The Baths Extensions.

Councillor Plumpton and the Turkish Baths. At a meeting of the Town Hall, Park and Baths Com- mittee it was resolved that the following tenders of Messrs Heeketh and Son. Limited, for the undermen- tioned painting, be accepted :—No. 1 —Entrance hall, Town Hall, and No. 1 and N ) 2 committee rooms. at £lOO ; No. 2.—Remaining portion of work inside Town Hall buildings, at £B7 51 ; No 3.—Outside Town Hall, and buildings, and gate rails, &c., outside Bank House, at £144 ; N ) —lnside work at Bank House, at £69 Alderman BOLTON moved the confirmation of the minutes, and gave some information with reference to the tenders of Messrs Hesketh and Son, and, in conclu- °ion, he contended that taking the Emma altogether they were very reasonable and the tenders ought to be carried out. The Local Government Board had held the inquiry with reference to the extension of the baths and were satisfied that the scheme for the Turkish baths Ought to be withdrawn as there were several difficulties in the way. Councillor SMETHURST seconded. Councillor BENNETT asked by what authority a resolution which had been previously adopted by the Council had been withdrawn? It might be wise or it might be unwise. He would not express any opinion,but as the Council discussed the matter on several occasions and had come to the deliberate conclusion to have Turkish baths no official or committee ought to take the responsibility of withdrawing it without consulting the Council. He and others were very much annoyed al what had been done. There w as another point. It seemed to him to be a curious resolution to close the baths on bank holidays and Walking Day at on. o'clock. These were just the days when the baths should be opened, as the public were then at liberty to make use ot them. He moved Mat the minutes relating to the closing of the baths on the days named be withdrawn. Councillor PIERPOINT seconded. Alderman BoLrosi said the committee had bad the matter under consideration, and had found that no one used the baths on the days named. 03CaSi ,nallv they had noisy swimmers, but they were better:kept out of the baths. Alderman HEATON : They are open at Warrington until one o'clock. We open till nine on Sunlay, and no one comes after that hour. Besides it is necessary tot the bathkeeper to have a holiday the same as anyone else. (Hear, hear.) The amendment was lost. Councillor ?Lumens then introduced the question of the Turkish baths, contending that the sch.me for their erection was withdrawn under very excep'icioal cii- cumstaoces—only the day before the Inquiry. The matter ought to have been brought under the notice of the Council before being withdrawn at the Local Guvern- ment Board irq dry. The Cmcioil ought certainly to have had a voice in the matter. Deputations had bren sent at great cost to other towns to see the Turkish baths. (Ironical cries of "Shame." and laughter.) The result was that all the expense had been thrown away by what had been recently done. The plans of the alterations and extensions were all complete and he con- tended that I' urkish baths could be built cheaper now than separately at a later period. Tne provision of these bitba was not a fad, and they ought to he within the reach of working men. They vv.uld be self-support- ing. Ile moved that the Turkish baths be proceeded

with, with the alterations to the existitur baths. The MAYOR said he could not accipt the amendment as it did n-it come within the scope of the minutes, but Councillor r.umpton would be in order in giving notice of motion for another meeting of the C )uocil as a dis- tinct in Aim].

Councillor FLU:UPTON : You will have gone on with the baths by that time. The MAYOR: You will be quite in time at the nett meeting. Councillor FLUINIPTON ; Very well, then. I cannot understand why the members of the Council have changed so soon with reference to the Turkis'a baths. Afderman BEATON : Mc reason for changing is that there would be a loss of £2OC a year to the ratepayers. Alderman BOLTON, in rrpicing on the discussion, said the committee were under the irnprrs.qion that the Turkish baths culd not be carried on at a profit. If the Committee could provide the baths and make a revenue they would be happy to do so. The motion for the confirmation of the minutes was then put and agreed to, Councillor Plumpton alone dis- senting.

div.head: 'llll4', EXAMINER, FRIDAY, JULY 5 1901
div.p: 'llll4', EXAMINER, FRIDAY, JULY 5 1901
Open Spaces.

At a meeting of the General Purposes'Committee, the report of the Open Spaces sub-Committee was read and approved. With reference to S. Janes Old Burial ground, the sub-committee report that the river wall is being re-built. The Manchester Ship Canal Company have provided two skilled workmen to assist. When the river wall is completed, it is proposed to take down the wall adjoining Koutsford-road,and to re-erect a portion of the same above the river wall, with an unclimbable iron fence at the top. The sub-Committee recommend that when the gravestones have been removed to the Cemetery as arranged, a row of trees should be planted along the river aide and portions of the groand should be planted with suitable trees and shrubs, and the remainder of the ground asphalted. It is not proposed to erect any fence to the front of Knutsford-road. In dealing with Orford-lane Recreation Ground the Sul:- Committee recommend that stumps should be erected opposite the end of all streets and passages abutting on the ground to prevent vehicles being taken over, provi- sion being made at the end of Blue Coat-street and Grounds-street for the removal of the posts when required. The sub-Committee are of opinion that the Markets Committee should be required to pay rent for Ithe use of the Recreation Grouna, aria that the money should be applied for the laying out and improvement of the ;round.

div.head: report 9711.9 adopted. A report of the proceedings respecting Warrington Bridge will be found in another column.
div.p: The report 9711.9 adopted. A report of the proceedings respecting Warrington Bridge will be found in another column.

Success of a Warrington Sunday Scholar. Some year. ago a lad belonging to the Sunday school connected with Emmanuel Reformed Epis- copal Church, expressed to the minister, the key. E T Reed, a desire to become a Foreign Missionary. The lad, Joseph Callan by name, was at that time employed by the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company as an apprentice to the iron mould- ing trade, and had to be at the forge every day at 6 a.m., the day's work ending at 5.30 p.m. At the suggestion of Mr Reed young Callan attended the Evening Continuation School at the People's College on three evenings in the week during one winter session, gaining a prize for good attendance Having thus shown that, he was in earnest in seek- ing to acquire the requisite knowledge to fit him for the career of a missionary Mr Reed began to give him gratuitous tuitional help in ereek, Latin; English &c., while at the same time Callan was actively engaged in Christian work as a teacher ; in the Sunday School, and as an active mem- ber of the Christian Endeavour Society. &c. In the course of time Mr Callan nad made sufficient progress to enable him to pa.s the entrance exam- ination at the Countess of Huntingdon's College, Cheshunt, where he has just finished the third 'literary yer of his college course. On the occasion of the recent annual meeting of the College held on June 27th, Mr Callan was awarded a certificate, of which the following is a copy :--'• Countess of Huntingdon's College, Certificate if Honour. This is to certify that Mr Joseph (Jallan, of Warrington, has diligently attended classes for instruction in Greek, English Literature, Logic, Psychology and Ethics, Hebrew and Homiletics, and in token of our approbation of the manner in which he has acquit- ted himself at toe pudic examinations Of tnese classes we present him with the Ist Certificate of the 3rd Literary year.(Signed) Owen hitehouse, MA, D 1), Principal, and Professor of Biblical Exegesis and Theology, Herbert T Andrews, B A, Professor of Ecclesiastical History and Theology. hrnest W Johnt•on, M A, Professor of English and Classics, William Johnston, MA,B D, Professor of Mathematics and Pnilosopy, T J Butcher, Trustee ! and Member of Committee." Mr Callan was also I awarded a prize of £5 for an exanninvion held last lEaster, in the study of the English Bible.

div.head: _ Gas Committee. Report of the Gas Committee. The Proposed Transfer of Offices.
div.p: _ Gas Committee. Report of the Gas Committee. The Proposed Transfer of Offices.

I The minutes contain the annual report of the Gas 1 Engineer (Mr Haddock) whidh was read and approved. It was published in Saturday's "Esaminer." At a meet- ing of the Gas Committee the following report of the sub committee appointed to report en the proposed transfer of the offices to Springfield was read and adopted "The sub-committee have fully kqaired into the pro- posed transfer of the offices to Springfield, and are of opinion that it is not compatible with the rfficient work- ing of the department to separate the general offiez• from the stores and fitting shops; that it is undesirable to erect new shops at Springfield, and that under the circumstances the sub-cersimittee cannot recommend the use of Springfield for office, for this department." I
_ Tne DEPUTY•MAY)II proposed the confirmation of r the minutes, Alderman HEATON seconded. . .

Councitlor 13ENNETT said he had Bot had time to go through the unsatisfactory report ot the semmittee, and he would like some explanation of the difference between this year's and last year's profits. He judged that there had been some serious falling off. The DEPUTY-MAYOR replied tnat coal Wll9 4s a ton more than in the previous year, and that bad reduced the profits. Councillor BENNETT : What were the nrnfits last year? Alderman FAIRCLOUGH : There was £5OO profit last year. The electric light had affected gas a little at the start and then they had to allow for had trade, which was responsible for • reduced consumption of gas. The minutes were approved. The Water Works Extensions. At a meeting of the Water Committee held on the 24th ,of June, it was resolved that the tender of Mr C tV ' Davenport for the erection of engine house and other buildings at the Delph-lane pumping station at £8.271 104, be ace- p'ed, and that the Chairman, D-puty-Ciaair- man, and Engineer be appointed to attend the annual *sleeting of the 3ritish Association of Waterworks Engineers at Birkenhead, on the 9th of July next. Alderman FeeNcolun proposed the adoption of the minutes, and said the committee hoped in a short time to give a complete list of every hydrant In the town. 11-ferring to Mr Deas' report on the filtering of Appleton water for trade purposes, he said it was necesiary to filter the water from Appleton as it would otherwise spoil the different products of many of the works which were very Isree consumers. Councillor JOHN EVANS 9econded. Alderman MONKS mentionea for the information of members, that a list of the mains and hydrants bad already been supplied to the Fire Engine Committee so they would now be only repeating what they bad done before.

The minutes were °steed. Proposed Extensions at the Electric Lighting Station. ' The Electric Lighting Committee recommended that the following tenders be an cepted in connection with the extension scheme :—Babcock and Wilson, Limited; of Renfrew, to sunpiv boiler, superheater, brickwork and pipes at £1,486 10:q Dick,Kerr and Company of Preston to supply steam engine and dynar..o at £4,413 ; the St. Helens Cable Company Limited, of Warrington and St Helens to supply cables and conduits litc at £6,870 7s lid Alderman MONKS, in moving the cenfirtnation of the minutes, statcd that the Council had already decided to carry out extensions at the electric lighting station and the recommendations were to give effect to it. The tenders recommended were not the lowest in any one case and they were not the highest. With regard to the boilers, the committee's hands were scrnnwhat tied because arrangements were made for tnis particular type of boiler and it would ha rather awkward to adopt any other type. There was, however, only • difference of £25 10a between the two tenders in question. With respect to the engine the committee struck out foreign firms and had to refuse the lowest tender because the firm had had no experience in the making of large dynamos. With respi ct to cables there was a great amount sf detail which only engineers could thoroughly understand and the Cable Company's tender was accepted on their recommendatinn. The tenders amounted to £12,769, which waa £250 less than the engineers' estimate.
Alderman FAIRCLOIIGII seconded, and the minutes were approved.

The Tramways Committee to Form a Deputation. The Tramways Committee recommended that the members of the committee visit the works of Messrs SI F Milne and Company, at Hadley, near Wellington, on the sth July, for the purpcs of inspecting tram cars. I The Town Clerk reported that he had recqived the sanc- tion of the Board of Trade for the borrowing of tbe sum of £66,050 for tramway purposes. Mr Woodward, of Messrs Preece ana Cardew, attended the committee, and submitted sketo showing the adaptation of poles for overhead equipment and for arc lighting. It was resolved that Messrs Pre eze and Cardew be requested to I confer with Mr Grimsdale on the subject, ano report to this committee. A sketch pan of a proposed new car shed a M.-ney -street works was submitted by Messrs Preece and Cardew, and it was resolved, that M'essrs Preece and Cardew be requested to report upon the ad.ptability of the existing premises for car sheds. The Mayon moved the confirmation of the minutes and stated that the committee proposed the first resolu- tion with the full knowledge that it was not in strict compliance with the recommendations of the Council in November last. He contended that it was in the interest of the Corporation that every memloix of the committee should be made as fully ace; minted with the detail; of electric traction in alf its departments, This was only one of three places suggested to te visited before the committee Itoalir decided upon the type of car to be adopted in their tramways. Be was glad to have the opportunity of correcting a public statement in the " Guardian " t,‘ the effect that the Corporation was going to pay £6,000 for their tramcars as against £5,600 by the Manchester Corporation. As a matter of tact the committee had not decided to pay any sum at all for cars. The order wts not placed hnd would rut be placed until the committee had personally inspected the three works and used their judgment and informa- tion for the purpose of advising the C)rporaticn h!ch

type of car finally to adopt. Ile felt it was due to themselves to protest against the circulation of such unfounded and mischievcus reports as ttie one in ques- tion was calculated to do a great deal of injury and cause misconceptions in the minds of people who were not acquainted with the facts, There was another matter. The " Drily Mail " published a paragraph that a certain contract given by the committe2 had been secured by an American firm and that the whole of the money was to be spent ia America, :Since the state- ment was issued, a contradiction had been made be the firm in question, pointing out that with the exception of a few details in the equipment, the whole of tins con- tract was being carried out in this country. Alderman MONKS seconded.

Councillor SMETHURST, in referring to the proposed car sheds suggested that the members of the Council should visit the old retort houses in Merry-atreet. Re (Councillor Smethurst) was convinced that with a little alteration they could be adapted for car sheds. Alderman BOLTON pointeclout that if the Committee insisted upon having everything new and at any cost there would be little chance of making .a revenue. The Mayon : You are agitating yourself unneces- sarily. It will ba time to criticise when we propose new car sheds.
Alderman BOLTON : You are doing everything in the dirk. This car shed should have been put in tba first estimate.
The MAYOR It was put in. Allerman BotzoN : It was not put in the first esti- mate.

The MAYOR: Now that you have made a statement without justification let me collect you. Alderman BOLTON : I was given that information. The MAYOR : Your information was not con ect. The car shed wee included in the first estimate, and formed part of the application to the Board of Trade which has been sanctioned. The Council wss not committed to a new car shed, and if the present buildings could be altered to suit the Committee's r( quirements they would be altered. Let the Council give the Committee credit for not wishing to spend the ratepayere' money unless absolutely necessary. The minutes were then passed. The Assessment of Land Values. 'Legalised Larceny.,'

The General Purposes Committee submitted the fol- lowing report of the Town Clerk on the land Rating (England and Wales) Bill:—This Bill provides for the separate assessment of land and the rating for local purposes of land values in boroughs and urban dis- tricts in Eneland and Wales. The annual value being- -4 per cent of the amount for which the land could be sold if there were no building or struaure thereon is to be inserted in the valuation list of the area. Every Town Council would have to levy a land value rate of not less than 50 per cent of the rate in the £of the total of the local rates levied on the hereditament com- prising the land on which such rate is levied. The land value rate would be payable in the first instance by the Occupier, but he would be entitled to deduct it from his rent. Any agreement to the contrary with the land- lord would be void." The committtee resolved that in the event of the bill being read a second time a petition be peem'ed to Parliiim.nt in favour of the principle of the bill.
the Mayor moved the adoption of the minutes. . _ _

- -- Councillor A J JOLLEY moved an amendment that the minute in question be not confirmed. He could understand persons, he said,who were quite honest but not well-informed supporting the bill, but he could not conceive of any man who was both hour st and well informed supporting it because its proposals were sub- versive to civilised society. It would be within the recollection of some members of the Council that on the last occaroon the subject was discussed he urged that in a short time the report of the Royal Commission on Taaation would be published. As a mater of fact it was published on the day he spoke and some of the remarks in the report bore on the question before them- The members of the Commission were unanimously of opinion that existing contracts ought not to be inter- fered with. The proposal of Mr John Burns to smash existing contracts was characterised as crude and I violent, and he (Mr Jolley) thought they were quite justified in saying so. As to the question of rating land in which there was no beneficial occupation there was a difference of opinion. Be submitted that no one having an adequate knowledge of local rating would maintain that a special additional rate in addition to the full local rates should be imposed. In his opinion it would be nothing less than legalised larceny. Honesty was the best policy for municiapalities as well as individuals ansi since the resolution committed the Council to a policy of petitioning in favour of what seemed dis- honest he moved the amendment.

Alderman BOLTON Fec9nded the amendment. He felt very strongly on rateable values. He thought everyone ought to pay rates but he did not think one person ought to pay at the expense of another. He thought the all very crude and very badly drawn. Councillor BENNETT said if it was legalised larceny to make people, who derived large sums from land values, pay something towards the expenses of the community he believed it was, at any rate, common sense. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) It seemed to him that there was a I large number of individuals who were the fortunate possessors of properties which had increased in value through no effort of theirs,and who contributed nothing to the welfare of the community either in public service or rates. If it was possible to get at them by the Bill mentioned be was in favour of it. The present rate- payers were feeling the burden of increased rates and he thought they ought to get at those who did not con- tribute their fair share to the well-being of the town. On a vote being taken the amendment was carried,l3 voting for it and 7 for the recommendation of the committee.
