div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The usual fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse, Dutton, on Tuesday. Mr J Stoke!' presided, and there were also present :—Messrs Alt Norman, T Reynolds, T Lea, J Douglas, T Wood (Run- corn Guardians) ; the Rural District Councillors, with Messrs George F Ashton (clerk). and W E Bough assis- tant clerk.)

AN 001ING FOR THE GIRLS. Mr. Cunnah reported that several ot the girls attended the Girls' Friendly Society Festival at Runcorn, and were well entertained. Mrs Maitland Wood kindly pro- vided a wagonette both ways. The House Committee bad passed a vote of thanks to Mrs Wood for her kind- ness. (Hear, bear.) THE VISITING COMMITTEE. _ _
-- The Ladies' Visiting Committee reported that s meet- ing was held on the 26:h June. The wards were visited and everything found quite satisfactory.

TELE PURE BEER BILL. Sir Cuthbert Quilter, M.P., writing under date June 19th to the Cierk stated that the Pure Beer Bill passed the second reading on March 27th by the large majority of 112. Every pcssible effort was made, without avail, to induce the Government to affLrd an opportunity for referring it, before Whitsuntide, to a standing Com- mittee which would practically have assured its passage ' into law this session, but Mr. Balfour had now under- taken to put down as the second order on tbe 26th inst. a motion for sending the bill to Grand Committee, and it was of the utmost importance that that motion should be:sucCessful otherwise the Bill must inevitr bly be lost this session, and it was unlikely that an equally favourable chance of passing such a measure would occur again. He therefore equested that the Board would ask the attendance and support of the local M.P.'s when the motion was brought forward. The clerk intimated, that the Board, having already passed a resolution to support the Bill,he had forwarded the requests to the local members of Parliament, and rt ceived a reply from Sir J'r Brunner to the effect that he hopes to be able to comply with the wishes of the Guardians in the matter ot supporting the Bill. (Hear, hear.) FINANCE. Mr S Woodward submitted the finances. Out relief OP% granted as follows: Runcorn £B6 ; Frodsham, £24 ; Budworth, £26. Making • comparison of the expenditure of the fort- night with the corresponding period of last, Mr Wood- ward, in a general statement, showed that the expenses of the house were more under the new Dietary Order than under the old. Taking the comparison as is stood the difference was something like £124 more on the quarter. The Master had also tound that he could work the alteration for loss Chats his first. estimated expenditure, but neverth3less it was a decided increase on the old system. Mr T Wright seconded the adoption of the report, which was agreed to.
THE HOUSE CONIMITTEE„

Admiral Jones Parry gave notice, that he would at the next meetibg give notice that Mr T Reynclds be appointed to the vacant chairmanship of the House Committee. He would also move that the salaries of the Master and Matron be increas, d. Mr Reynolds stated he felt that there were mans older members of the Board more entitled to the honour, and would be obliged to Admiral Parry if he left ^him out. Further discussion on the matter was deferred to the next meeting of the Board.

div.head: ABSENCE OF THE CLERK.
div.p: ABSENCE OF THE CLERK.

Mr Ashton asked for leave of absence from the neat Bcard meeting. The Volunteer Battalion to which he was attached was encamping on Salisbury Plain from the 13th to the 27th July next. The encampment was a long_way off, and it would be difficult to return.

-Mr-Woo'dwaid proposed that the leave of absence be granted. Several guardians scconded. The Chairman : All in favour. Carried. Mr Pilling : If here is no time mentioned ; is the leave of absence for ever ? (Laughter). I Mr Linaker : The time is from the 13th to the 27th, I The Chairman (to the Clerk) :We hope you will enjoy 5 ourself, (hear, hear), and come tack safe.

Is it well that Liberals An Appeal for Liberal Unity, should magnify their differences? Ought they 'not rather to unite upon the matters about which they are agreed? These are the questions which are suggested by a careful reading of the speech of Sir HENRY CAMPBELL-BANNEMIAN at Southamp- ton. The speech of the right hon. baronet itself supplies an answer. The Leader of the Opposi- tion has been much blamed for sitting on the fence. It is easy to repeat glibly a familiar catch phrase, which acquires by use a species of fnscina- tion which becomes infectious. But it may well be asked what other course was possible in the present situation. As Sir HENRY said at South- ampton, leaders like Mr. GLADSTONE are a fruit that does not grow on every bush. There can be little doubt that a fighting leader would have succeeded only in making a complete wreck of the party in its present wilful temper. In his own words, the present leader has not allied himself with any extreme section. He has endeavoured to act in co-operation with those who were prepared to apply Liberal principles with moderation and with judgment, with those who were prepared to subordinate their personal prejudicies and preferences to the general inter- ests of the party; and it is difficult to see how a party can be carried on in any other way. It is the extremists on both sides who have given the trouble, and it has always been so. A middle course, then was the only possible one for a leader in present circumstances, and it must depend greatly upon the degree of loyalty shewn by the body of sound, sensible Liberals who have the in- terests of the movement at heart whether the party will survive the dangers of disruption which at present beset it. It is to be feared that pure jealousy and selfishness are at the bottom of a good deal of the mischief, and it is only by the cultiva- tion ef a spirit of magnanimity that any progress towards conciliation and subsequent concentration can be secured. If there is to be any question of "capturing" the party for this or that section, the damage done will be more far-reaching in its effects than any amount of energy, however well directed could offer compensation for. Sir HENRY made no reference to Mr AsourTifs dinner, which has been the cause of so much disquietude. Probably he had .an impression that the dangers which it threatened had been very much exaggerated, and, indeed, no other view is possible after the very sensible letter which Mr. ASQUITH has pub- lished. His avoidance of the subject was there- fore its wisest treatment, and the only one con- sistent with the tone which he was endeavouring to impress upon his audience. What the right hon. baronet has done is to appeal to Liberals inside and out of the House of Commons for a united party, and, as we have before declared, union is only possible where mutual forbearance and tolera- tion show the magnanimous spirit. As Sir HENRY has said, there are some points, even with regard to the war, upon which the bulk of the party are peafectly united. There are also the other ques- tions which, he says, a man of Mr. GLADSTONE'S energy, will, and force of intellect would h eve arranged differently from the methods of the pre- sent Government. There are the questions of temperance, of rating, of national education. These still lie before the Liberal party, a rich field for enterprising action. Let them determine to
I

act together in these matters, strongly, sympa" thetically, energetically, and in the putting forth of such an effort they will derive fresh internal strength, as well as increasing influence in all their surroundings.
SECOND only in import Rating of Land ance to the question of Values.

National Education is that of the rating of land values, and it is a sub- ject upon which the public mind:ought to be edu‘ cated with a view to coaingencies which may arise in the not very remote future. We now have it on the authority of the minority report of the Royal Commision which has been sitting since 1896 on the question of Local Taxation that the subject is one which may well engage the atten- tion of the administration. The minority who have reported are Lord BALFOUR of Burleigh,Lord BLAIR BALFOUR, Sir EDWARD HAMILTON, Sir , GEORGE MURRAY and Mr &tam% They are not men who can be fairly charged with prejudice-- 1 against the landed interests, and their authority : carries weight which cannot be ignored. They - are of opinion that the rating of land values, that is the value of town lands and building sites, for local purposes is both equitable and expedient. It seems a singularly strange anomaly that CO contribution to local rates is made by the very class of property which owes its existence to the 1 modern system of local taxation. Were it not for lighting, cleaning, paving, draining and other police and sanitary arrangements which make town life so amenable as compared with rural life, there would not be the large influx of population to our towns that there is. indeed without those modern provisions so necessary to the healthy exis- tence of large communities the huge aggregations of people that form our large towns and cities , would be impossible. The improvements which are the constant object of attention by our Towu Councils and local authorities are the attractions which draw in the rustics to the towns,while they contribute also to the increase of wages- which - form a corollary to this advance in civilise' ' 1 tion. But they are all paid for out of the rates. The extension of towns and cities resulting from these combined forces is the 1 lever which the ground landlord uses to bring grist to his mill. It enables him to put a fictitious value upon the land he owns, and which he leases for a longer or shorter period for building purposes. The period is generally a shorter one, so that when the:lease expires and the land falls in to him or his successor, carrying with it all that it bears, he may reap a further harvest by an increased ground rental. It is little short of a scandal that the land laws of the country should permit these fre- quently recurring leases with huge profits reverting, to the owner who has done nothing to earn theta, ißut so long as the system is permitted to exist I surely the wealth thus created may be expected to bear its full share of the local burdenS I which have created it. At present the small shopkeeper, the struggling trader end the householder, are the persons who have to hear the everincreasing burden. The ground landlord who is the first to benefit by the clearing of sluLfls! the maintenance of drains, repairing of roads and building of bridges, pays nothing in his caPacitY of landowner. The result of the presents is that land values approximate a fifth of the ren-f tat and about a fourth of the assessable value ° house property, and they escape rating. To if dude them in the assessment roll would be heti'. equitable and profitable. It would considerahl lessen the burden on the present ratepayers. 15e; sides it ought to have a deterrent effect on the 6,., very farseeing mild speculators who hold up the' land until the value has been raised by searcitY to a figure that makes houses dear and rents PO' portionately high. It is in the interest of tlif3 community in every way, that some restrictioe should be placed upon these self-seeking monor lists who in their operations become the enemies of the public weal.

• We have heard before, without positive convie; tion, the statement that the rays of the sun nothing whatever to do with "sunstroke," and fear that those who are once ;nore repeating will gain few converts. Such a pronouncemee" goes dead against all our pre-conceptions. Pride rebels against it, for if it is true the human race has for centuries been using, with a full faith their efficacy, protections which are of no avel: As the miller, in the old riddle, wears his whir hat to keep his head warm, so' or rather contra wise, the British soldier wears his white helmet t,e keep cool the same indispensable portion of his anatomy. Even the case for the puggere,: goes, and there is no further teed for tu" thin-haired son of civilisation to be enviott: of the luxurious and entangled grooLtic, which protects the brain-pan of the tlev't savage. The contention is that it is not the be of the sun, but the humidity ot the air which 1,1 the enemy; and the suffering which those oblige' to be in the streets of New York have had to !II; dure is pointed to in proof,there being no gnestlo about the fact that in that city almost comeietgt saturation of the air is common enough in sum%) weather. However, if external moisture is Es' immediate cause, still behind this is the heat of the sun which raises the saturation point of the 11 and brings about the condition of thingszo terriblL enervating to the dwellers in cities. Doubtless Iheat is less likely to cause collapse than one which the atmosphere resembles a vapour ban I Still adequate protection for head and neck ag,ainst sunshine is as indispensable in one condition I the air as in the other.

IT is singular that those savants. who distres! themselves so greatly about the possibility of tb: exhaustion of the earth's coal measures in aar°,l two hundred years have never alarmed mankia with stories of the approaching rarity of other lilt; portant natural substances. Coal may be describu.; as in a sense still in course of production-10 smaller quantities, doubtless, than in past perira of the earth's history, and at a rate so low for all practical purposes mankind may be saia t be living—and living, too, in an extravagar, manner—on its coal capital. Surely, howeyea there is a likelihood of all the gold, or, "d. least that which can be profitably worl‘eo, becoming exhausted before the two cel.o tithes are over. Tile inauguration of a scheme of Artisans' Dwell- during the week at Bath, marks an important Parture r that is going on in various parts of the °vinces,aq well as in the city mentioned. The itl ceremony in this case was performed by Tweedmouth. It is on the moral and phy- a„-11 welfare of the people that a nation's greatness guprosnerity depend. The sanitarian has already tet.°lltributed largely to accelerate progress towards .26 desidersted standard, while there still remains utUch for him to do, not only on his own account, bat in co-operation with other authorities to whom la a certain sense, is committed the welfare of those who dwell, either from necessity or choice in centres of large population. The housing pro- blem promises more and more every week to be one of the most exigent. as well as the most im- portant, with which our national and local legisla- tors will have to deal during the early part of the twentieth century. Parliament has been rather housing in the facilities granted for the adequate I.plising of the less well-to-do classes, and that ?eing so it is all the more welcome a sign that the peal authorities are beginning to realise it as their bounden duty to make the most of such powers as they already possess,

It is some time since one saw any raturn of the num- ber of fatal accidents resulting from the practice of qCling in our public roads and thoroughfares. A little light was thrown upon the matter, however, 11, 7 a Birmingham paper which directed attention Ant week to five different fatal accidents that oCcurred in a less number of days, within the area nf its own local circulation. Four of them, how- ever, related to cyclists themselves, whilst the fifth .kwall a lady killed by a cyclist,in the sense of having !Alen run into and dying afterwards from the • Injuries received. The cyclist comes in for severe Criticism and many opprobrious epithets at times, bin as regards four out of the five cases referred to tUB tables were turned for once. It is impossible to offer any excuse for the furious " scorcher" who 'Whirls along the highways,or rushes wildly through the public streets at serious risk to life and limb in the way so often witnessed. But what to do in the 'Way of prevention is not so eas,ly said. Whatever restriction may be suggested, it is teat with the argument that if adopted it would be in restraint of trade. •

It is being urged in certain quarters that in this Country the tendency is to unnecessarily restrict the driving and the speed of motor oars, to the alleged disadvantage of the iron, and steel, and Other industries, as well as to hinder and reduce , Yie facilities these vehicles would otherwise intro- quee into the national system of locomotion. Then, as if to tone qvn the harshness of the comparison, it is otoksively: suggested that what is wanted in this IlUtry is less freedom than there is in France and 41'the Continent generally, and some relaxation in 0 law which governs the motor monster's move- ents. has brought us." It was an able, concise address, Pitting plain facts in plain language. Mr Cameron touched upon most things which have occurred in tie history of the present Government, including ord Salisbury's "graceful concessions," the doles to favoured classes, education, and of course, the War, There is still as much, if not more, interest 1.13. the war and its causes as in anything else ~IraPerial, and Mr. Cameron's views were dl royghtfully listened to. Ile expressly stated his belief that if there had been no Rhodes and no great Icl mining companies seeking huge dividends tuare would have been no war. We are quite in ,accord with Mr Cameron. There is a distinction ,?etween a Government which plunges into war lor love of gold and conquest, and one which is talaled by astute, unscrupulous capitalists to take 11,P arms in apparmit self-defence. That distinc- tion Mr Cameron seems to appreciate. It is not °ne,however,which at all excuses the Government. The Government has been weakest when it has ap- ared strongest, and weakness of this type is ann. ost criminal. In fact an admirable sermon tl.lght be preached on the wickedness of weakness, With the present Government for an example.

, Mr. T. Birchall seems to have leaped before he tas looked, in writing the letter which appears in another column. Our leaderette last week is the !aildest criticism compared with Mr. Birchall's .7Lagrant misconception and violent abuse of it. 'We do not in the least plead guilty to " blind Prejudice' or "gross inaccuracy," and our corn- tents were based on the special description of the meeting which appeared in what we venture to "Isider the soundest Liberal paper in ~ 140ndon. The meeting was unquestionably a Packed meeting and the resolution it Passed was peurile, while the importation °L 700 " stewards " "from Battersea" was direct menace to the free speech which Mr. alr.chall claims justly as the right of every Briton. •Lials right we explicitly stated even the pro-Boers 'were entitled to, and Mr Birchall's allegation that we said they had no right to give public expression to their opinions is entirely inaccurate. We know Mr. Birchall well enough to believe that this ads- Statement is inadvertent, but the whole tone of fi_la letter indicates a superficial reading of, and a etasty judgment on the remarks we made last week.

How many children were tired but happy nn eriday nigtit,in Warrington? Ninety-five per cent at least we should think, for all those who partici- Pated in the numerous school treats cannot have icleen anything else but happy on such a glorious and there were very few left in town after ;17311- The streets wore quite a deserted aspect, trP for the bands of older folk who flitted from a ot-i-", to pub,” like the busy bee and the flowers, all '`laB,B symbolic of nature. It was alaci Walking .Day, and one that repaid ampiy for the disappointments of the three during some previous ones when rain fell part of the time. The morning pro- cessions were "beyond compare," particularly those of the Catholic schools, which, ornate in 'rerything, made the most of so festive an occa- Van. One cannot praise the parents and teachers 00 much far the great expense and trouble they had manifestly taken. Viewed from the Town Hall steps the charmingly attired youngsters proces- aianing across the lawn looked more like sylphs or Wood-nymphs than inhabitants of this work-a-day !vorld, and the opinion was unanimous that never 4ad a prettier spectacle been seen in Warrington.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
MEMEY MISSION TO SEAMEN. RUNCORN.

The first of a series of open-air concerts in con- nection with the Mersey Mission to Seamen, was given on the recreation field, Holloway. Runcorn, by the Weston Point Salt Works Band. There was a fair number present, and these amused themselves with football, cricket, &c., while the band went through an interesting programme. The proceed- ings were kept'up with much spirit till nine o'clock, FIRE AT WESTON WORKS. On Saturday a fire broke out at the Weston Works, but happily the men on the spot were able to extinguish it without the services of the fire brigade. The outbreak, it seems, was discovered in one of the sections of the works which is at present inactive,being located in some old dry rafters which formed ready fuel for the devouring element Thanks to the energy of Mr James Tudor, the manager, and a number of the staff the fire was put out before any considerable damage had been done. Information as to its origin is lnot to hand. RuNConN ANGLERS' ASSOCIATION. The members of the above association plied rod and line in a very interesting contest at Weaverton, near Chester, on Wednesday aftPrnoon, under the captaincy of Mr S. Bailey, Regent-street. Capital sport was enjoyed by all, and two flap roach were Captured—one by Mr Bailey (10/ ounces), and the other by Mr T Bate (10k ounces). The prizes were secured by: Mr S. Bailey (19 ounces); Mr T. Lea (11 ounces) ; Mr J Bate (10k ounces). LADIES SEWING MEETING. The Ladies Sewing meeting of the Runcorn Wes- leyan Circuit,who have their meetings at St. Paul's, invariably hold tbe July fixture as the pic-nic of the year, and visit Halton. Therefore, on Wednes- day last a good number left by brake at about 4 o'clock in the afternoon, and arrived in Halton in time to partake of a generous tea pro- vided by the Halton friends. Through the kind permission of Mr Walker, the Castle and Grounds were thrown open to the company and an enjoy- able evening was spent there. FIRE AT RUNCORN. About 4 a.m., on Friday morning, Constable Gilpin, discovered a fire which bad broken out in the loft of some stables belonging to Mr Savage, butcher, and adjacent to his High-street premises. At the time a valuable horse was in the stable, and this was very gallantly rescued by the constable. an alarm was raised, and the Runcorn Fire Brigade were soon on the spot, and took steps to prevent further damage and to stay the course of the con- flagration. This was speedily affected, but not before a quantity of hay and straw and the upper portion of the building had been destroyed. The origin of the fire is unknown. THE RUNCoRN SAVINGS BANK. Mr 13 Imison presided over the half-yearly meet- ing of this Bank, which was held at the Bank Offices on Wednesday evening last. The actuary, Mr W Handley, read the notice convening the meeting and submitted a statement show- ing the half-year's business. Since November 20th last, the number of deposits made was 1,471 ; cash deposits, .26,462 13s 94 : there were 645 withdrawals representing .28.378 153 101 There had been one transfer to another bank of £25 ; ten purchases of consolidated stock for de- positors at cost of £1.144 us 6d ; one sale of stock realizing £977. 91; 64 dividends on stock credited to depositors. £57 us 64 ;and one transfer of stock to the Bank of England. There were 2,104 trans- actions and £16366 0544 represented the turn-over for the half-year. The auditor's report and certi- ficate 68 to the correctness of the accounts, as well as the receipt of the National Debt Commissioners were examined and found eatisfactory.-241,107 Is Id was invested with the National Debt Com- mi3sioners ; and £395 93 31 was the balance re- tained by the treasurer, or a total of £41,502 Is 44 to the credit of the bank,

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The Roy Canon Wood presided over the usual monthly meeting of this Board, held on Thursday evening last. The attendance included :—Messrs E Imison, F J Nor- man, W Handley. 3 Littler,W J Cunningham, 9 Taylor, Rev Father Chambers, Mr J W Liglatburn (clerk), Mr A Lightburn• "THE EDUCATI IN BILLS°. A letter from the School Board 'immolation raised a discussion as to the propriety of supporting Sir 3 T Brunner's Elucttion Bill. Mr F 3 Norman, as an educationalist, and a supporter of the Government. proposed. that the Board should support Sir J T Brunner's Bill. It was the one thing which would tide the nation over the disastrous effects of the Cockerton judgment. Mr W Handley supported, contending that School Boards, being the parties purely respo-osible for the elementary education of the country, should protect that interest, apart from anything else. Then there was the question of loyalty. Mr Taylor also .upported the motion. Mr Imisnn moved an amendment, that the Govern- ment he asked to proceed with their Eaucation Bill. Mr Littler seconded _ _ _ •

The Rev Father Chambers was more inclined to wait, land see what would hapn,n to the Government Bill Fir- ing its process through Committee; yet, he was inclined to support the amendment. The Chairman having characterised the "Elueationat Crisis," as it was called, as something which a eertain class of people were inclined to magnify. failed to see why they—because they were a School Board—should he obliged to throw in their weight practically against the present Government. It had also been pointed nut, by Mr Norman, that the Government Bill Wag not likely to go through Parliament, but to his way of thinking there would he less likelihood nf Sir J T Brunner's Bill becoming law. On a vote being taken, Messrs Norman. Taylor and Handley supported the proposition, and mess" Littler, Cunningham, Rev Father Chambers, and the Chairman the amendment. It was also decided to send copies of the resolution to Sir J Gorst, Mr Balfour. and the Duke of Devonshire. A CORRECTION. Mr F J Norman pointel out that the local Press had reported Mr Raison as having stated that" the rate was Z5O less than last year, and therefore the rate Payers had good grounds for coniTralltdation." El- ton!: the strongest exception to such an impression being created. The members of that Board knew, well enough, that the rate was exartly the same as last year. The Chairman thought that Mr Norman had a com- plaint against the Press, and would do Pest to write to the Press. That was the best remedy. Mr Imition, however, appeared as anxious es Mr Norman to have the matter clear, and remarked that what he said or intended to say was that the precept was £5O less than the previous precept. Mr Norman retorted it was strange that the whole Of the reports should make exactly the same mistake ; tut even accep'ing.Mr Imison's statement, that he used the word " precept " and not " year," he still wished to Point nut that it created an altogether wrong impression. For, the tntals remaining the same as the last year, there was no ground whatever for congratulation. A etTrESTIOII OF RATE. Mr F J Norman then raised the question: "If £1,700 In 1.808 rertrasentad 9i in the £on the rate how was it that £2,050 (£350 more, for the last year, still repre- sented a 9d rate ? " Some discussion followed, hut no one seemed perfectly clear of the isgueg, se that eventually it was mutually agreed to continue the argument just before the election Comes on. In the meantime the clerk was instructed to procure the documents necessary for solving the problem.

div.head: EXAMINER' FRIDAY. JULY 5 1901.
div.p: THE EXAMINER' FRIDAY. JULY 5 1901.
RUNCORN NOTES.
[BY A CORRESPONDENT.]

The Runcorn School' Board at its ordinary monthly meeting indulged in what might be termed a pro- fitless discussion, at the end of which they decided to write to the responsible members of the Govern- ment Sir J. Gorst, Mr Bilfour and the Duke of Devonshire, uraing them to push forward the Government Education Bill. That was on the Thursday night; On the Friday morning, it became generally known that the Government Bill would be withdrawn, and that Sir J. Gorst would formu- late another. One wonders now, whether the Government Bill would have been withdrawn if the Runcorn School Board resolution had reached its destination a day sooner?

The Runcorn Volunteers go to camp. on Salisbury Plain, from the 13th to the 27th of July next, with their regiment the 2nd Earl of Cheshire's. The camp will be a brigade camp and include several other regiments.

The question of Baths is now bein--• raised, let us hope, for the last time, in Runcorn. I feel that the effort if taken up in the spirit with which it is initiated by the workmen and directors of the Highlleld Tannery, will result in the baths question being settled satisfactorily There is no better way of getting what is requisite, than that of " helping one's self " thereto. And, if the people are determined to pur- sue that policy, everything will be alright. I might not agree with the Chairman when he wants to convert the Market Hall into the baths,for I love old institutions ; but I am with him when he says "jet us have a feasible scheme and secure the sup- port of the public."

The Free Church C3uncil meeting, held at Bethesda schoolroom, illustrates the trouble ahead for the present Government if they take too long to decide on something to lessen the friction in educa- tional circles. Runcorn people scarcely understand the full extent of Government Bills; but they positively do understand grievances with which they have to put up and aq far as the locality pas will endeavour to rectify them.

Mr Norman, it is very evident, intends to knock the bottom out of the cry" down with the rates! " long before the day of election comes off; and the answer to the conundrum he propounded at the board meeting, the other evening, will simplify matters to a great extent. The Liberal party may be dead to the country, and the leaders may be at loggerheads; but, in Runcorn, we have evidence enough of a vitality of such strength and healthi- ness on the Education question, that it becomes a pleasure to contemplate it.

div.head: RUNCORN URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: RUNCORN URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of the above Council. was held at the Town Hall, on Thursday morning. There were present: Messrs Rif Poseett (chairman), S Taylor, W Handley E Irnison, D Biebrown, M J Sweettnan, J Wilson E Gatley, J if Stikeld. J W Lighthurn. T Dean, with Mr F A Like (law alerk),Mr E Marqball (cecretary) Mr J Wilding (eurveyor) and Dr F McDougall (medical officer.)

div.head: DIRECTIRSIIIP.
div.p: THE DIRECTIRSIIIP.

Mr S. Taylor, who moved the adoption of the High- ways and Buildings Committee minutes, referred to the pleasure it gave him, to move the confirmation of Mr. Posnett's appointment as director on the Widnes and Runcorn Bridge Co., for the ensuing three years.
Mr W. Htn-dley ;mended and the proP3sltlon was carried.
The Chairman responded. THE RATE OF INTEREST.
The Finance Committee published a copy of the following letter in its minutes : Ecclesiastical Commission, 10, Whitehall-place, London. S W, 13th June, 1901...

" Sir,—Your letter of the 11th inst has been laid before the Ecclesiastical Commissioners, and I am directed to inform you that the Commissioners will be prepared to advance to the Ruscorn Urban District Council the sum of ten thousand pounds (210,000) at the rate of interest of three pounds twelve shillings and sixpence interest and per cent per annum. The pay- ment of principal to be made by 60 half-yearly payments of principal and interest combined,which would amount to about £2 153 per cent upon the amount of the loan. Your obedient servant, ED. C. BOCK PORTER. Mr W Handley wished to maintain the views he had previously expressed. He illustrated how the present system—the annuity system—of borrowing ranney and repaying it, was so much better than the sinking fund principle, and how it would be a saving to the Council of a considerable sum. £16,848 would be the full amount the town would have to pay if they earned nothing at all by the bridge. Mr Imison, in reply, pointed out he was right in his contention that the anticipations of the supporters of the scheme had proved fallacious. Me Handley had put the recayment down at £528 15; 51, and the fallacy of the figure was demonstrated by the fact they had to pay £549 103 10i ; or £2215; more than Mr El andley said they should. He wished to point oat, however, that for every penny of money they borrowed, fne every minute of time, they were called upon to pay 33. per cent. Mr Handles, : And for every minute of time we get interest on our money. The matter then dropped: ANOTHER PORTRAIT. _

div.head: Mr D Bisbrown intimated that aaother portrait, that a Dr Steele bad been secured, and added to the gallery of " portrtits of past chairmen."
div.p: Mr D Bisbrown intimated that aaother portrait, that a Dr Steele bad been secured, and added to the gallery of " portrtits of past chairmen."
THE BATHS CII7EBTION. A HANDSOME OFFER.

Mr E Marshall read the following letter :—" Highfield Tannery, Runcorn, July 3rd, 1901. The Secretary, Runcorn Urban District Council. Dear Sir, our atten- tion having been called to the necessity and want of swimming baths in Runcorn for our employees, we are anxious that something should be done in this direction on their behalf and also that of their wives and families, who we understand at present have no bathing facilities whatever. We have therefore authorised our Managing Director, Mr R H Posnett to contribute on our behalf the sum of £250 for the purpose of erecting baths in Runcorn—if your Council 'deem the need to be so great as we do. The only conditions we name are :—(1) That a satisfactory scheme of at least £l,OOO be carried out and contributions to that amount obtained : (2) That the working people and children of the town should have the opportunity of using the baths at popular prices. —Yours truly, for the Highfield Tannery Company, Limited,G W Mackie, secretary." Mr W Flandley thought it was a very important letter and should be referred to the General Purposes Corn. mittee.

The Chairman agreed that the course suggested was a wise one. He wished to explain, however, that the letter was prac- tically his own, and it came forward officially from his firm. Everyone of them must have felt, especially latterly, there had been rather more Coroners inquests held on children in the district, and they had been paying a rather heavy price for not having bathe in Runcorn. Some time ago he was approached by the workmen to do something to secure them a bath for the works and they would Day some- thing weekly, and had subsequently browalot the matter up at the Directors' meeting. The feeling expressed there was that it would be best to subscribe to a scheme for baths for the town, rather than provide I something for one private firm (Hear, hear.) I Hence the letter was formulated. The two most import- ant factors in the consideration of the Market I Hall scheme were that there was the building,and all that was rrquirel was to add the bath accommodation and secondly, a magnificent water supply ran quite dose thereto, viz., the Sprinch water: He felt that if they as a Council would only bring themselves to the front in the matter and set the ball rolling the people of the town would take it up. Men who were willing to put their hands in their pockets for the relief and soldiera' funds would again do their best to provide their town with baths and bathing accommodation. He had had the opportunity of con- sulting MrS Taylor, and wish hi.' mend sympathy, he said be was willing to contribute ElOO. (Hear, hear.) Mr S Taylor seconded. Mr J W Lightburn supported the resolution, which was carried unanimously.

div.head: NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.
A Former Chairman Presents His Portrait.

A meeting of the Newton-in-Mikerfield Urban District Council was held in the Town Hall, Earlestown, on Monday evening. Mr Collingwood presided and there were also present : Dr Patterson, Dr. L ahem, Messrs. C B F Borron, J W Emmett, W Gilmour, J Simpson, W Thompson, E L Bent, E T Evans, T Ormand, %vita A Bowes (surveyor), and C Cole (clerk). THE LATE MR. GREGORY.
A letter was read from Mrs Gregory and family ack- nowledging the vote of condolence pissed by the Coun- cil at the last meeting on the death of Mr Gregory, a former inspector of the authority:___ _
PRESENLITION OF A- POR raatTi

The following letter was read from Odr W F Gooch, a former chairman of the old Board of Commissioners : " I have great pleasure in presenting to the Urban Dis- trict Council of Newton-in-Ytakerfield a life-size portrait of myself to be hung in the Council Chamber of the Town Hall in memory of my lo og connection with the Newton Commissioners as chairman, which I trust the Council will do me the honeur to accept. I have to thank my co-commissioners for the very kind support they at all times gave me during the time I was chair- man and whichlhave left many pleasant memories. Mr Gilmour said he had great pleasure in moving that it he accepted. Mr C B F Rorron, in seconding, said he would like to say a few words as one who served under the chairman- ship of Mr Gooch as an Old Commissioner. He could assure them that he had many pleasant memories of that time. He deeply regretted that Mr Gooch left the neighbourhood for he was a valuable public man. He only wished they had more men of his calibre in the district. Mr Gooeti devoted himself for the benefit of those among whom he lived and he (Mr Borron) was glad to think chat the portrait of Mr Gooch would be I hung in the Connell Chamber. It was decided to acknowledge the gift. TECONICAL INSTRUCTION COMMITTEE. At a meeting of this committee a letter was read from Mr J. W. Emmett, the hon treasurer of the Viaduct Institute Technical Instruction Committee sating that the County Council Grant of £BO 103. had been paid direct to him instead of to the treasurer to the Council, as heretofore. It was resolved that the Clerk write to _Ube Clerk of the County Council and ask for his reason for the departure is the mode of pay- ment. A letter was read from the Secretary of the Viaduct Institute Technical Instruction :Committee stating that the nembers of the committee elected by the respective authorities for the year ending the 31st May, 1902, were as follows :—Representatives of the Council: Messrs C B F Borron, C.C., E T Evans, J N Patterson and W Thompson. Representatives of the Viaduct Institute Committee of Management : Messrs J W Emmett, J.P., D Barcroft, P Connor, W Davies and C W Emmett. _ _
Dr. Patterson moved the adoption of the minutes which were agreed to. _ GAS COMMITTEE. _
The report of Mr. Bowes (the engineer pro fern) for the past month was read, from which it appeared, that, as instructed, be had investigated the practice followed

in- the -non-lighting of street lamps in certain roads dur- ing the summer months, and that, in addition to the printed rules,a custom has been followed for many years —in the interests of economy—of leaving unlit the lamps in the outer districts between the middle of May and the middle of August, /11,99 t of the lamps being brought into the Gas Works for repairs and painting. Ik was resolved that M. Bowes be instructed to report further with respect to the lighting of street lamps in the district. The Chairman reported with respect to the stoppage of the supply of gas on the night of the 14th inst. and Oat as the cause arose from an accident no blame was attached to anyone, but rather that the foreman was to be commended for the way in which he iiad dealt with the matter.
The minutes were confirmed on the proposition of Mr Thompson. _ WATER COMMITTEE. _

This Committee recommended that the gas foreman (Mr Hoggard) be directed to select a suitable man from among the men employed at the gee works to be speci- ally trained as a relief engineman at the pumping station, so that he may. when required. take charge of the engine and pumps at the water works and be held responsible for efficiently and satisfactorily discharging the duties whilst there, and to relieve one of the enginemen from duty each Sunday and at other times when necessary, and that the ordinary rate of wages to be paid to such man be left to the Chairman of the Gas Committee. Also that the enginemen at the water works be allowed one wok' s holiday with pay each year. Confirmed on the proposition of IMr Boanorr. HIGHWAYS AND SANITARY COMMITTEE. PROPOSED SEWAGE SCHEME.

This Committee resolved that the Clerk be instructed to write Mr A C Leslie (Lord Newton's agent), and re- quire him to fence the land in Wargrave-road known as "Thompson's Pit." It was resolved that the Surveyor be instructed to prepare specification and estimate Df the cost of beautifying the Town Hall. The following building plans were approved and passed, viz :—Board of Guardians of the Warrington Union relief offices, corner o! Market-street and Nelson-street. J Price, 11, Earle-street, A Widd, 198, Common-road, two dwelling houses Emmett's Brow, W Bates, 121 a, Earle-street, W H Walker. 279, Crow-lane W, two dwelling houses, Emmett's Brow. The Surveyor reported to the Committee with respect to the proposed sewage scheme as follows:—That many streets in the-district are waiting to he completed. In January, 1898, the Council' applied for powers to raise money for street-making, but the application was re- fused ortJaccount of the condition of the:Sewage Works at that time. Thereupon the Council determined to try • the effect of bacterial treatment and with- out 'making any structural alterstione, converted the old settling tanks at both sewage works into bacterial filters.slThese were completed in August last, and gave such satisfactory results that it was thought desirable to complete the works on this system In December, 1900, the Council made an informal application to the Local Government Board for permission to spend £2..000 on an extension of the scheme. To that the Local Government Board replied, January 26th, 1901, that before any scheme could be considered by them it must include the provision of land for irrigation pur- poses, and certain proportions of filter beds as related to the flow of sewage and storm water were required. The provision of about 20 acres of land of suitable quality and at suitable levels is a very difficult matter, and is complicated by the numbers of railways, canals, and streams in the lower part of the district. There are many works existing, some within a few wallas of here, where land hag been 110 ebtained and is not used, as it is not necessary Co obtain an effhent which fulfils the legal standards. As was pointed out in May, 1898, a new scheme to meet the present requirements of the town, and disregarding cest or the fact that two sewage works now exist, would be to take all rhe sewage of the town to the lowlying land south of Vulcan, and there treat it bacterially. Tills would cost approximately, £18,160 The sewer from the west sewage work; would be two miles lone, running by the side of the Sankey Brook, and would be a costly and difficult piece of b work. It can only be avoided by obtaining a seem.* re piece of land somewhere near the west sewage works and connecting Vitriol-square to the 4gsewe works,erinE and thenatnett's- brow.l utilizingthisw he artedone the soheme would be Out in portions, existing w cost would he impreximately P,10,310. If it were found unnecessary to use land for irrigation. the above esti- mate would be reduced by £7,100 The disadvantage of the latter scheme is that there would be three separate points at which workmen would he engaged daily and supervision recinired. His recommendation to the committee was to adopt the latter scheme and include it in provision for treating the efil -vents on land. It was resolved that the Clerk be instructed to write to Colonel R Pilkington, upon th. question of the Council's application to the Local Government Board for their sanction to the borrowing of money for the extension of the sewage naheme. and engnire when the report of the Royal Commission on sewage disposal will he pohlisheri, and that Councillors C B F Borron, W Coiling wood, T Ormand, together with the Clerk and Surveyor, be appointed a deputation to wait upon the Local Government Board with respect to the Council's application for their sanc- tion to borrow money for the extension of the Sew- age scheine.—The Medical Officer of Health attended the Committee and reported with respeet to the tyros of scarlet fever in the district and as to the want of accorei. mociation at the Warrington isolation Hospital. Fre ad vied the Committee in the interest of the health of the inhahitanta of the necesaity of providing an isolation hospital for the treatment of local cases It was resolved that Councillors C B F Borron, W Collingswood, Dr Latham, T Ormand and Dr Patterson, with the Medical Officer of Health, be appointed a Suh-Cemmittce to consider the question of the provision of an isolation hospital for the district, and to obtain information as ta Cost of it; erection and management. It was also re- solved that the question of the voluntary notification of phthisie i's referred to the Medical Officer of Health. The Chairman proposed the adoption of the minutes. Mr Simpson seconded and the proposition was agreed to. THE ASSESWENT OF THE TOWN HALL..

The Clerk reported tn thn GenPral Putnam!' Committee that thp gross value of the Town Hall Buildings having been recently inereased by the Assesstnent Committee of the Warrington Union from MOO' to £3OO, he had, on behalf of the Council, appesled against such increased assessment, and on the 7th inst anneared before the Assessment Committee in support of the objection. HA stated that the receipts for the lettings of the eo,ms at the Town Hall since its erectimn had been : 1897, £95 3a 61 ; 1898, £3S 16s - 1899, £94 5s 1900, £37 Is 6d ; 1901, £4B 31 31; and that if the basis of the assessment was the annual value of the building for the conduct of

the Council's business, then he thought that £lOO would be a sufficient sum ; and that that amount, together with the annual amount of the lettings (which would shortly be decreased by 14 per annum—the am nut paid by the Guardians for toe use of an office at the Town Hall for relief purposes), should form the gross annual value—the assessment thus not being altered. The Chairman of the Assessment Committee stated that the assessments of all the public buildings in the Union had been revised, and :hat in the opinion of the committee the assessment of the Town Hall, Earlestown, was not too high.—The Clerk called the attention of the com- mittee to tthe fact that the Town Hall, Newton-le- Willows is not rated to the general improvement rate, the highway rate, or the water rate,—The committee also resolved that the Clerk be instructed to write to the Clerk to the County Council with respect to the making of a bye-law by that Council under sec ion 17 of the Local Government Act of 1883 for the prevention and suppression of betting in the streets. The Clerk stated that at a meeting of the committee held that afternoon,it was resolved that the report of the Commissioners' deputation to Lord Newton be deleted land that the report of the sub-committee be referred back for further consideration. The Chairman moved the confirmation of the minutes. Mr Gilmour, in referring to th minute relating to the assessment of the Town Halt, N swton, stated that he asked the question in committee whether the Town Hall at Newton was not assessed whilst that at E ales- town was. The clerk admitted that the Newton Town Hall was not assessed, but he gave the answer very un- willingly and It had to be dragged out of him. The Clerk pointed out that his report on the matter was laid before the committee. Mr Ormand said the remarks of Mr Gilmour were obviously unfair to the clerk. They were most untrue and most unjust. Mr Gilmour was entirely under a wrong impression._
Mr-Grilm. our : No. Mr Ormand : The minutes ars a perfect record of the committee.
The minutes were then passed, Ur Gilmour dissenting.

I The following letter was received from Mr Edward Yeld in reply to a request for increased postal facilities : —" With reference to the memorial of the Newton-in- Makerfield Urban Digtrict Ccuocil, dated the 3rd inst,in which application is made for an additional evening de- livery of letters in Newton-le-Willows, and the establish- ment of a sub-nost office at Newton Common, I am requested by the Postmaster-General to inform you that the pregent number of deliveries is that usually afforded at places of similar six, and amount of correspondence as Newton-le-Willows, and there are no special circum- stances which;would warrant the department in incurring additional expense in order to provide an exceptional service in that town. If generally desired by the resid- ents of the district, arrangements could be made for commencing the last (or third) delivery at or about 5 30 pm instead of 4p m, and, should the Council he in a position to show that such is the case, instructions will be given accordingly. The question of establishing a new sub-post office at Newton Common is still under consideration, and the result shall be' communicated to you as soon as a decision hag been arrived at--I am,sir, your obedient servant, EDWAUD YELD." div.head: RUNCORN NURSE FUND.
div.p: THE RUNCORN NURSE FUND.

1 What has proved one of the most delightful and successful garden parties ever held in Runrorn with a philanthropic object, was the one given by Mr and Mrs R Abel, of Croyton Lodire.Runeorn,on Wednesday after- -1 noon. The object was the very laudable one of swelling the Runcorn Nurse Fund, and its popularity, as well as he popularity of the host and hostess, was testified to by the large number of townspeople present. The whole of the delightful grounds were thrown open, and the large crowd thoroughly enjoyed the walk round. Of course, in every likely spot was some attraction or device for enticing the " coppers" from the pockets of the guests into the desired channel. Gramaphonefs, concerts by Gipsys and Pierrots, and other side shows ; a maze ; 1" 'Artful dodgers" ; cocoanut shies ; and even Aunt Sally was pressed into the service. Tea was served on the lawn, and the sight the company presented when seated was really charming, In the evening. the Run- corn Orchestral Society played for dancing in the tennis court, where the jollification continued from 8 to 11 p.m., at which time the strains of the National Anthem signalized the close of the proceedings. Mr Horace Handley conducted the band, and thole musical programme was crisp, cheerful and exhilerat- ing in every respeo".—The masters of ceremony, &e, included:—Mensrs W Crosby, A Abel, F Abel, F Han- cock, W T Crosby, T Priestley, T A Little, George Hewitt, J Horsfield, J Dvlsen, Frankling, T and J Briscoe, and T Brown, whilst Mrs Abel and the ladies of the family were responsible for the refreshment depart ment. rhe whole was an immense sucessa and realised a good sum to hand over o he Nurse Fund.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

SAD FATALITY AT FRODSUAEd.-..011 Friday afternoon at the Frodsham Police Court, an inquest was held by Mr J C Bate, coroner, on the body of Thomas Foster, who met with his death whilst driving a horse and lurry near Frodsham, on Wednesday.—John Hancock, a waggoner at Netherton Hall Fula], stated that on Wed- 1 nesday last week he went to Frodsham with a lurry and' two horses,for the purpose of taking a number of school children to Claim Farm, Kingswood. The furry was packed with children, and witness was in sole charge. Deceased came to him along Woodhouse-lane, No con- versation passed, but deceased walked beside him for a short distance. Deceased then went on. and took hold of the head of the horse at the front. Witness told him to leave go, and he refused. Deceased had not led the horse far, when he made a stumble and fell down. They were going downhill at the time, but 'they were not trotting. The horses were both young. Both wheels went over the deceased's back. The deceased was not sober, and witness could give no reason why he went to lead the horee, When he fell he nude no effort to get up. The foreman of the jury, Mr Jones, chemist, who was on the scene at the time of the acciaent, said that flancock's evidence was entirely Jorrect —The Coroner, in summing up the facts, said the direct cause of the accident apneared to be the man's condition. He seemed to have made no attempt to save himself, and be was of opinion that no blame attached to the driver.— fhe jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death "and exoner- ated the driver from all blame.

The brakes not acting satisfactorily, the conveyance was drawn down one of the steep inclines at such a great speed that one of the horses lost its folting and was dragged a con- siderable distance before the ether animals could be drawn to a standstill. It was then found that two of the horses had received serious injuries, one of thorn having to be shot directly afterwards. It was a miracu- tousescape for the party.

SAD BURNING FATALITY AT EARLESTOWN. On Wednesday at noon a child named William Shaw, about two veers old, son of Thomas Shaw, a Core Maker. of 344, Wargrave-road, Earlestown, was so shockingly burnt that he died half-an-hour after receiving the injuries. The child was just recovering from an attack of scarlet fever, and was in bed in the fr-mt room, in which a fire was burning. The mother left the room for a few minutes and hearing screams she hurried back and fuund the child had scrambled cut of bed, and Ro t to the fire.lt was wearing a flannelette frock which had beclme ignited, and the deceased was shock- ingly burnt about the head and upper part of the body. Medical aid was summoned, but the efforts to save the child's life were of no avail.

div.head: INTERESTING OPERATIONS BY VOLUNTEER CYCLISTS.
div.p: INTERESTING OPERATIONS BY VOLUNTEER CYCLISTS.
Acting as Dispatch Bearers.

The members of the Cyclist Section attached to the Warrington Volunteer Corps acquitted them- selves creditably in some interesting operations which were carried out on Saturday. It had been arranged that the men should carry a dispatch from Warrington to the War Office in London. The idea originated with Lieutenant Haslam,who is in com- mand of the section and who assisted in an experi- ment of a similar kind in Australia where cyclists Conveyed a message from Sydney to Adelaide. The permission of the War Offie to make the experiment reached Warrington on Thurs- day. Lieutenant Haslam immediately developed his plan and the cyclists who were to take part were despatched by train on Friday to various points along the route. Tneir object was to prove the practicability or otherwise of cycliata carrying a message from Warrington to London in the event of communication being cut off. Twenty men connected wita the section were engaged in the experiment. They were posted at different points along the route in c ouples, and the message was handed on from point to point about 20 miles apart.

The first two cyclists, C3lour-Sergeant Mainley and Corporal Bailey left the town at seven o'clock on Saturday morning and passed the message on so Privates Cooke and Perks at Four Lane Ends, Tar- porley, at five minutes past eight. 3he time occu- pied in covering the 214 miles was therefore 1 hour 5 minutes, an excellent start. The next place where the message was handed on was at Woore. Privates Broady and 'tinge took charge of it, at 9.20, and conveyed it to Weston-on-Trent, that place being reached at 10.55, when Corporal Holloway and Private McCue went on to Watling-street, Lichfield, ariving there at 12.18, and passed the despatch on to Privates Davenport and Hulme who took it to the Harrow Inn, Watling-street (a little beyond Atherstone), arriving there at 1.35. From thence it was conveyed by Privates Warren and Gornall to Kilsby which was reached at 2.50. Here it was banded to Privates Rooke and Jewk•?s who passed it on to Privates Hatton and Osborne who were in waiting at Stony Stratford, at 4 30. Dunstable was reached at 6 o'clock where Privates Hodgson and Bickerstaff received the message and passed it on at St Albans at 7.5. Privates Haigh and Longdin here received it and passel the message in at the War Office at 8.30.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN• [BY A CORRESPONDENT.]
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN• [BY A CORRESPONDENT.]
Cricket.

Newton are exultant over the easy defeat of Earlestown by a Liverpool eleven on Saturday. It will be remembered that Newton when they jour- neyed to Aigburth gave an excellent account of themselves, and very easily defeated the Liverpool team. Earlestown went to Aigburth with high hopes, but those were 'speedily dispelled, as their attack was much too weak for the Liverpool bats- men, who closed their innings with might wickets down. Some excuse may be found for Earlestown in the fact that they were without Aiderson, their principal bowler. In the batting they were also lamentably weak, and they had to retire defeated by over 100 runs. It is evident Earlestown will have to look round for some new blood, or take some means of improving the players they now have.
The second team had a remsrkablv easy thing on with Bolton Grammar School (Old Boys) and won very comfortably.
The Newton team are playing a very consistent and successful game this season. They paid a visit to Eccles on S3turday, and won in very easy fashion.

-- The second team, however, was not so successful, the Eccles men proving much too good for the Newton team. Of course this may be accounted for by the fact that Newton were short of two or three of their regular players.

The Police and Press match is likely to yield fair sum in aid of the charities it is intended to sup- port. The tickets have been well sold, and some fair donations have been received. Altogether it is computed that something over .£2O will be cleared. With such a result as this, the Police and the Press should be encouraged to make the encounter an annual one.

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
"COULD DO THE SWORD EXERCISE."-AN OBJECTIONABLE
RA iLwer PASENGEIa.

John Banks, a hawker, whose address was given as E 4, Hanover-street, Manchester, was brought before the Warrington magistrates on Monday, on the charge of interfering with the cr,mfort of passengers travelling on the Cheshire Lines Railway on the 16th June, con- trary to the Company's byelaws.—Superintendent Simpson said that on the Sunday in question the de- fendant was a passenger from Liverpool to Manchester by the 9.35 p.m train. He entered a third class cem- partment in which were several soldiers and two gentle- men named Richardson and Ward. After the train had started, defendant noticed the soldiers and remarked he had once been a soldier. He then commenced to brandish a stick saying that he could do the sword exercise. He used the most filthy language and when one of the gentlemen remonstrated with him be called him a "pro-Boer." When the train reached Farnworth he commenced t act in a most disorderly and indecent I manner. He was asked to give his name and address and he replied that it was " A Wilson, 29, Duke-street, Man- chester," which was subsequently found to be false. He was allowed to proceed, and on arrival at Manchester he assaulted Mr Richardson, for which be was locked up, and had just served 14 days' imprisonment.—The Bench imposed a tine of 40s and costs, or, in default, a month's imprisonment with hard labour. He went to gaol.
A TRANSPYRT COMPANY FINED-DISGRACEFUL CONDITION ( F B ARGES. __. . .

At the Warrington Police Court on Monday before Mr F Monks and otter magistrates, the Manchester and Liverpool Transport Compt.ny Limited, Exchange Buildings East. Liverpool, were summoned for failing to I keep the boat Esther in a clean and habitable condition as rtquired by the L)cal Government Board.—There. were similar charges with respect to the boats Alert and Alice Field. Mr Stanley Wilson (deputy-Town Clerk) prosecuted on behalf ot the Corporation acid stated the facts of the case at length. c mtending that a breach of the Canal Boats Acts, 1877 and 1834, had been coin- ittPd. With regard to the Esther, he stated that on the 21st June, Inspector Nornaan went to Bishop's Wharf and there boarded the boat. He went down the

--- aft-cabin which he found was registered for three persons. The berth which should have been used by . the master and his mate was unfit for use and the men had to sleep on the seats of the cabin. The woodwork was very dirty owing to a want of paint and the cabin was unfit for habitation. So far back as December last

• yea-r-, the first inspection of the boat was made and a summons taken out. A representative of the company appeared before the Court and a fine of 5s was inflicted. • complaint note was sent and acknowledged by the company, but nothing appeared to have been done since, and the boat was in the same condition as when the line was inflicted. With reference to the Alert, lispeCtor Norman found the woodwork of the cabin dirty from want of paint ; in his opinion it bad not been painted for some year. fhe boat required thoroughly overhauling and painting. Notice was served on the 23rd Octobertast rear wben the first inspection was made. In thiq case also a complaint note was sent. - Other communications with the company took place, . . .

and when the Inspector last visited the boat it was in a worse condition than it was when first visited. The Inspector found the aft cabin of the Alice Field in an uninhabitable condition, not being weather proof. The deck above was defective, and the water ran through and oettrd the bedclothes. The cabin was also in a dirty condition, He (Mr Wilson) did not know what excuse the company could have. They bad be given every opportunity to put the boats right and had not 'done so, and he, therefore, . prersed for the full penalty.—lnspector Norman gave evidence in support of this statement. _.. —A representative of the company said, all the boats had been registered within the list two years. The company had 14 barges, all of which were registered under the Canal Boats Registration Act, and he con- tended that the company bad done everything it was necessary for them to do. Each boat was painted every twelve months,but he was afraid that there was wanton • destruction on the part of the men. A .fine of 101 and costa in each case was inflicted, and ?dr. Monks remarked that if a notice was sent in future and no attentim was paid to it the full penalty would be inflicted.

Moattiag.—Before Messrs G L Davies and F 3 Norman. " AN If NiaINE DRIVER AND HIS lIIILK."—This was a case in which David a Guilford an engine driver ill the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Company, was alleged to have stolen a quantity of milk, the property of Mr Robert Shepherd, of Park Farm. Sutton, whilst in transit on the Ist of April last.--Mr Brassey, solicitor, Chester, pro- secuted on behalf of the Cheshire Milk Producers' Associa- tion, and Mr Quillen. solicitor. Liverpool, defended.—lt appeared that the defendant descended from his engine at Sutton Weaver Station with a can three-parts full of tea. Having seen on one of the milk tankards he passed a small quantity of milk, which had evidently oozed oat of the venti- lating holes at the top,he asked someone whom he thought was in charge of the tankards. if be could have it and was told "Aye," He then tient the tankard forward and poured about two tablespoon's full into his tea.—The witnesses for the prosecution contended. that Guilford had poured milk out of three different tankards, taken a drink, and again poured milk into his can.—The Bench in dismissing the case pointed out to Guilford there was no doubt that he had taken milk which did not belong to him, but in their opinion there had been no felonious intent. RE3W-ICABLE LADDER THEITES —James Wilson a painter of Runcorn, p eaded guilty to three cases of larceny of ladders and elected to be summarily dealt with. The first case gone into showed that the prisoner had on the 22nd of June taken a ladder belonging to Mr Hugh Hasp billposter, in the employ of the Runcorn and Widnes illiposting Co. valued at 193. and sold it to Mr Jonathan Horsefield for 4s ed alleging he was bard up and wanted food. The second case showed Wilson had borrowed a ladder valued at 45, from Sarah Ellen Littler, 16, Leinster.gardens. In this case he told Miss Littler that he required the ladder to paint a couple of cottages. The ladder not being returned, resulted in inquiries being made, whereon it was found to have been sold to Mr John Pennington, Greenway-road, for 38 64.—The third ladder, it appeared had been stolen from Mrs Samuel Baaley, the caretaker of Camden Wesleyan Chapel, and was the one which was / usually used for window cleaning. This was valued at 2s 64 and had been sold to Robert Collings. Laburnum Cottage, Higher Runcorn, for a small sum.—h. each instance,prisoner , had told "his customers," the ladders were his own, and alleged being in want of food as the cause for him selling ' them. All the transactions had teen carried out between the 15th and 28th of June.—Prisoner was sentenced to seven I days in each case, sentences to run consecutively. UNHAPPY MARISIAGES.—John Raddican was summoned on / the information of his wife under the Married Woman's Act. 1195.—Mrs. Raddican, swore they had been married 13 years, and resided at Riley's Row, Weston. During the whole of ' her married life, she had been ill-treatel, and cruelly used, by her husband. On the 24th June last, he unprovokedly gave her two black eyes, and knocked her about the place / until she could hardly walk. She applied for a separation and maintenance order. Her husbani earned 255. a week as a labourer at VVarrlngton. There were three children, one , with her father one with his father,and one with themselves. —Defendant, who appeared under the inficence of drink, did not deny the allegations of his wife.—The Bench granted the ' separation, and made an order for maintenance of 10, a week, Mrs. Raddican to have the custody of the child.— Joseph Denning. of Runcorn, was sued by his wfe Emma Denning, for £4 21. arrears on a maintenance order granted , Bth May.—Defendant declined to pay, and was committe for a month.

A BOY BIFICHED.—BamueI Leigh, a oy of about 13 years, Pleaded guilty to stealing 631ba of old iron, valued Is the property of Mr John Wiliam Perdvals'-lane, Runcorn, on Friday June 28th.—Defendant was seen to fill two old sacks with old scrap iron. ones ' which. containing 21Ibs. he sold to Mr Howard, marine store dealer, for 23/4d. The lad stated be gathered the old iron from a heap of rubbish by the locks. —Constable S Rowlands testified to the bay's apprehension. and to the recovery of the property.—Superintendent Pear. eon stated the boy had no father, and bad been before the court in April last, when he was sentenced to receive 6 strokes of the birch for stealing coal.—The Bench, consider- ing that a fine would be borne by the mother alone, and be no punishment to the boy, ordered hum to receive 6 strokes with the birch.
CLAIM AGAINSI THE FILESMITHS' ASSOCIATION.

At the Warrington County Court on Thursday,last week before his Honour Judge Howlands,B.C. William Stuart Jolley (administrator of the estate of Benjamin Jolley,of Hatton,filesmitit,deceased) sued Samuel Wright,Edward Roberts and John Appleton (trustees of the Warrington District Filesmitlee' Assuciation) for £lO, "di ath bene- fits " alleged to be hue to him on the death of his father and mother.—Mr Jenkins represented the complainant and Mr Browne appeared for the defendants.—Mr Jenkins, in opening the case, said the late Benjamin Jolley had for many years been a member of tte War- rington and District Filesmiths' Association. The object of the association was the application of the subscriptions of the members for their mutual support in case of being out of work, for the support of the old and infirm, and the decent interment of members and their wives on death. Recently a rule was passed deter- mining the amount ot benefit money to be paid to the relatives of deceased members at £4. Benjamin Jolley's wife died on January i:h of last year, and on the same day Mr Jolley's son made application for the death ben- efit due to his father. A meeting of the Committee of the Association was held at the Mason's Arms to consider the application and Mr Jolley, jon, was told that as at present they had no funds in band except for strike purposes (a strike was then in pro- gress) the money could not be found to pay the death benefit. Subsequently he made further applications,and in reply to a letter which be wrote to ate secretary,Mr James Battersby, he was informed that a resolution had been passed by the annual meeting " that we do not entertain " the appeal made by Benjamin Jolley for his wile's death money, she having died at a time when there were no funds in hand. Therefore no death money can b paid." Subs' quently he met the secretary who told him that they had now some funds in head and he had better apply for the money. The money was not paid. Unfortunately Mr B Jolley died and then application was made for another £4 death benefit. A letter was received by the son stating that the committee were of the opinion that there should be a declaration signed by Jolley and his brAhers and sisters to the effect that no further action legal or otherwise should be taken with reference to the claim for the mother's death money. In reply Mr Jolley declined to make the declara- tion and proceedings for the recovery of the two death beneets were instituted.—It was now stated that £4 93 bad been paid into court by the defendants, in settle- ment of the first claim.—A long legal argument ensued with reference to tha second claim, Mr Browne stating that the plaintiff was present at a meeting of the society when it was resolved that all death money be suspended—Plaintiff denied this.—The defendants ultimately agreed to offer plain- I tiff £1 lOs in settlement of the second claim, and this offer was accepted:
