WARRING ON BRIDGE.
Proposal to Rebuild it Defeated. Interesting Discussion at the Town Council Meeting.

An important resolution was submitted at the meeting of the Warrington Toil] Council on Tues- day evening by the General Purposes Committee td the tff ict that scheme No. 2 described in the report. of Mr John J. Webster, dated the 30611 October, 1900, for the construction of a new bridge over the Mersey, in place of the e,.:isting bridge be adopted. Toe scheme alluded to was for the construction of anew bridge and increasing the width of St James- street to 60 ft as far as Water-street. The work would include the removal of the existing bridge the material to belong to the contractor and to be used up in the new structure when possible, with the consent of ;the engineer; constructing new abut- ments, wing walls, Sze, constructing and erecting new steel superstructure, consisting of eight arched ribs 150 feet clear span, steel spandrels bracing, flooring plates, ornamental cast iron parapet rail- ing, cornice, outer spandrels and feur lam.) stand- ards; wood block paving on roadway, and grano- lithic pavement on the footways; the roadway to be 40 feet wide between the kerbs and the two footway+ 10 feet wide each from parapet to kerb. The bri lge had to be constructed in accordance with drawing No 3, at estimated cost £17,789 10s. To re-constructing the north approach and the south approach, including the widening of St. James-street as far as Water-street, was estimated to cost £998 16s. In the c :urea of a report on the proposed widen- ing, Mr Webster says it can be done by building in cantilevers on each side of the bridge and then ex- tending the width of the roadway by the widths , now occupied by the footways and the parapet ' Walls. The roadway is now 201 t between the kerb- stones, the footways about 401 t wide, and the thickness of the parapet wall 14in, so the greatest width possible for the roadway would be 301 t 4in; the footways 71t 61n wide would be carried by the cantilevers on each side of the bridge. "This arrangement would, no doubt, Ito a certain extent relieve the traffic, and it would be an economical way of doing so ; but I take it there are other considerations to be taken into account. In the first place although the traffic would be relieved, it would be only partially so; and the increased width would certainly not accommodate the present traffic during the busy times of the day with either comfort or safety; and when the double line of tramways are running with probably two cars abreast on the bridge, tne increased width of the bridge would be totally inadequate for the traffic. In the next place it must be remembered that there are practically five roads, each with its own traffic, converging on the bridge ; and for this traffic to be satisfactorily dealt with, the bridge should certainly be at least as wide, if not wider, than the widest of the converging streets. Even supposing the increased width would accom- modate the present traffic, the rapidly increasing population and trade of the town would in a very few years make it absolutely imperative that taore accommodation should be provided, and the money ' thus spent on the temporary relief would practi- cally be lost. Apart from tte utilitarian and economical considerations there is the al ithetic point of view. The old bridge has undoubtedly good lines, and is an interestmg structure ; if, how- ever, the cantilevers are fixed to the eides,it would necessitate the removal of the stone parapet wall, the cutting into the string courses, and the sub- stitution of overhanging cast-iron railings, thus completely spoiling the character of the structure, and in fact converting it into what would be to very many, an eyesore. As so much is now being done to improve the town both architecturally and otherwise, this view of the question deserves to be taken into consideration."

Mr WEBSrER. proceeded to state that after taking all these points into consideration. and the present river traffic, he was of opinion that the best plan would be to erect a new bridge on the site of the old one. The MAYOR moved the confirmation of the com- mittee's recommendation.

Councillor SMETHURST moved an amendment that the resolution of the committee be not con- firmed. He said the committee proposed to spend the sum of from .£lB,OOO to .£20,000 on a bridge and he should like to know a:refit they were going to get for the money. Ile pointed out that at the present time the width of the bottom of Bridge-street, from wall to wall was 49 feet, and tne bridge proposed to be erected was 60 feet, Why in the world were they going to build a bridge 60 feet wide when the main street which they had just widened was only 49 feet? On the other hand if they adopted the alternative scheme suggested by Mr Webster, and erected cantilevers on each side of the bridge, the width would singularly enough be only a few inchesdifferent from the width of the street. There was a proposition to build a new bridge over the river near the Stag Inn Swing Bridge, in connec- tion with the new road at Arpley. A short time ago a proposition was brought before the Council to construct a bridge at Howley and they spent a considerable amount of money in buying property for the purpose* The MANOR: We have the property on the other side. Continuing, Councillor SMETHURST argued that if these two, bridges were erected it would con- siderably relieve the traffic over Warrington Bridge and there would be no necessity to spend such a large sum of money. He was certain that if plans sent ntohCo o of the alteration by the erection of cantilevers had been presented at theen tl meeting, g, told the him thatun Council he wld was not have voted for the pulling down of the bridge. The other day a g so disgusted with the proposal to pull the existing bridge down that if he (Councillor Smethurst) wanted £lO to stop it from being pulled down he could have it (cries of "Have you got the .£10" and "Divide it"). Councillur TINNION seconded. Councillor PLIMPTON supported. He also was of the opinion that a plan ot the alternative scheme should have been submitted at the meeting. The MAYOR : We have not got it. In his report Mr Webster says ;-1 have not made a drawing of the proposed cantilevers, not thinking it necessary as they are so simple in construction and can be easily imagined; but no drawing could possibly show the effect these cantilevers would have on the appearance of the old structure, and if anyone has any sentimental feeling towards it,probably send- ated with his boyhood, he would receive a rude shock when be saw the proposed alterations carried out. Councillor PLIMPTON : We will have a rude shock when we know what we hive to pay for the bridgp. (Laughter.) Continuing, he contended that the cantilevers would look quite as well as the new bridge, and would serve the purpose just as well. The present span was quite as wide as the channel in which the vessels sailed. Some people were very economical in some thinga,but he believ- ed that if the alteration was carried out it would would just as well as buiLing a new bridge,answer for Warrington for the next sw er andth e pwuor d fifty years. Councillor JAMES EVANS said he would like to know whether, since the dredging operations had been com- menced, there was not more headway for vessels under Warrington Bridge than before. The MAYOR : I should not like to say. It is not a point that affects navigation at all. It is not so much a question of headway as of width. The headway is not material. Councillor Evaais : I think It is Very inater.al. The MAYOR: 51y point is that the difficulty in naviga- tion with regard to the central arch arises more from want of room than headway. The headway means only a question of time for the vessels to wait, but the want of ordinary room against; a swift current is a very impor- tant matter indeed. Councillor EVANS said that if this was one of the argu- ments In favour of the scheme it had not been used in the Council. Councillor PLIMPTON : That is all the argument there is. Councillor EVANS said that if the headway was as good as ever he did not see how the cantilevers were going to create any fresh difficulties in the navigation of the river. It seemed to him that the difference between the altered structure and the new structure so far as roadway was concerned was a matter of 15 feet. So that if they considered it from that standpoint they were gainins very little for the expenditure. If they were considering it from the standpoint of navigation let them say so and consider it on that point. He under • stood that the Board of Trade had sanctioned the laying of the tramways across the present bridge and if that I was so he did not see the necessity of urging the ques- tion for a little time. It was like a great deal of other things—it would keep a bit. He th(refore supported the , amendment. Councillor Fonsnaw thought the expenditure was so great that it would be better if the matter was deferred and he therefore supported the amendment. Alderman BOLTON said cantilevers were very un- siehtly and were very often dangerous, and might also obstruct the waterway• He contended that Warrington Bridge, being the principal bride° rye! the Mersey be-
tweenidanchester and Liverpool, ought not to bea disgrace to Warrington and ought to answer all re- quirements.

- Councillor & J JOLLEY said the whole thing resolved itself into a financial question. If someone came forward with £20,000 and toid them to build a bridge there would be no difficulty at all. He thought that if the Corporation intended to expend £60,000 or £70,000 on tramways they ought to see that the service was well worked. If there was to be a safe and frequent service over the present bridge it was evident that something would have to get out of the way. They had to think of the safety of passengers and also of the vehicular and rivet traffic. No one disputed that the new bridge would add to the safety of the river traffic and also add VBr7 , materially ta the safety of road traffic. In round figures there were just a million passengers cross the bridge per annum and according to estimttes of the Borough Surveyor there were about half a million cyclists and three quarters of a million vehicles. If all these foot passengers paid a penny each and each vehicle iji to cross the bridge it would in one year more than pay for the cost of the new bridge. His other point was that if each of the passengers and vehicles lost ten seconds each time they crossed, owing to the congestion of the present traffic and they estim- ated the value of the time at only a shilling an hour the value of the loss of time, independent of the vexa- tion and annoyance, would exceed the Interest and sinking fund on the new bridge, so that even on the lowest grounds it would be economical to have a new bridge. He felt very strongly that they ought not to oppose the scheme in any narrow spirit. He had said nothing of the casualty lists which would probably be expelienced if the trams ran over the present structure. From every point of view there was something to be gained by the erection of a new bridge. He was quite aware that the Board of Trade hal sanctioned the laying of the tram lines over the bridge, but he was also aware that without proper supervision the trams could not be taken over with safety. It would mean employing a staff of police- men on each side of the bridge andlthe passengers would lose far more than ten seconds in crossing the bridge. Councillor BENNETT pointed out that one never heard any objections to the scheme so long as it was expected that tho County Council would be willing to pay a con- siderable portion of the expense. He understood that the town was better off by being a County Borough and if a new bridge was desirable before it became a County borough it was more desirable now, and it was becoming increasingly desirable every day. At present the bridge was only 23 test wide, being 12 feet Less than the statutory width of residential streets. At the present timei the congestion was very serious and was bound to become more serious when they got the electric trams. They ought also to do what they could to improve the waterway and thus increase the river traffic and benefit the town. He pointed out that it was not exactly the width of Bridge-street that they had to consider, but the fact that five streets converged upon the bridge and poured their traffic over it. He charac- terized the proposals to add cantilevers to the present bridge, as ridiculods, and pointed out that it would involve a considerable cost of maintenance. There would be no economy in the scheme. He proceeded so speak of the his orical associations of the bridge and said that without the bridge there would have been no Warrington. He contended that the new bridge ought to be thorougnly adequate to meet all requiretnen:s and fully "presentable," even if it involved an extra three farthings or a penny in the pound. Councillor BURTON said he had never heard Councillor Bennett advocate anything unless it involved consider- able expense. (Laughter.) His (Councillor Burton's) opinion was that if a new bridge was built they would have another eightpence in the pound and more. The present bridge would be quite adequate for the trams. There were other things which were more important and more necessary than • new bridge: For instance there was Sankey Brook. The MAYOR: Oh, please— Councillor BURTON : I know you will say "Oh please." You live at Stockton Heath. (Laughter). The MAYOR: Sankey Brook is beyond the scope of the diacussion_.
Councillor StriaTosi : If the Corporation are prepared to spend limey let them spend it in trying to abate nuisances.
The MAYOR: At Stockton Heath we have the blessing of the Ship Canal close to us and it is quite equal to Sankey Brook_._
Councillor BURTON contended that the matter mighl be left over.

Councillor TINNION said he seconded the arneedmeet because Mr Webster's report said the alternative scheme was an economic way of dealing with the question. He contended that a new bridge was not necessary. Since the bridge was first proposed the conditions had very much changed. When it was first proposed, three authorities besides that Council were expected to con- tribute to the maintenance and construction of the bridge,the Lancashire County Council, Cheshire County Council, and the people who used the waterway. These bodies had now rrfused to contribute and be thought the time was inopportune to erect a new bridge at the expense of the ratepayers of Warrington. The figures quoted with regard to the traffic over the present bridge wanted a great deal of discounting. They were taken in the summer months, the time most favourable for traffic, and he did not think it was fair to multiply the number obtained by 52 and say it was the amount of traffic for the year. To erect the bridge at the present time would be throwing money away, because a very handsome bridge could be made of tue present structure Only one tram line was to be laid across the bridge at present. He was of the opinion that the total cost of a new bridge would be nearer £30.000 than £17,000. By erecting cantilevers they could make the bridge ample for Warrington for 20 years. Councillor GREENING supported the committee's recommendation and pointed out that in his report Mr Webster said " Apart from sentiment, I am strongly of opinion that the proposed widenieg of the bridge would be totally inadequate to accommodate the present traffic and that of the immediate future ; and that the fact of the proposed widening being an economical arrange- ment should not weigh much against any proposal for providing ample and safe accommodation for probable traffic. Taking all these points into consideration,and the present river traffic, I am of opinion that the best plan would be to erect a new bridge on the site of the old one." Continuing, Councillor Greening said the policy of wait and wait was a wrong policy. They in Warrington were suffering very heavily owing to the poticy of pro- crastination adopted by their forefathers. He pointed out that in a short time they would have to pay a higher price for the property required than that asked to-day. It was not right for representatives in that Town Coue- cii to think of every penny a public improvement was going to :lord. They built their hospitals and gasworks, sad widened the streets for the good of the community and the benefit of the town, and it was not right for the sake of a penny in the pound, to thwart and stop this necessary public improvement. Councillor WILLIAM Roman said he was in. favour of a new bridge, but he did not think that the present was the opportune time for it. They had a cumber of large schemes before the public' which were being carried out and be thought they ought to have a little breathing time before embarking upon further expenditure. It was necessary that the mem-1 boars of the Council should have more information beforel committing themselves to such a large scheme. Person- ally he would like to see a plan of the suggested can- tilevers as be thought it would help them to come to a decision. Alderman MONKS said he did not think the trams would add very much to the traffic of the bridge, in fact he thought they would tend rather to diminish it. At present the louses stopped on the bridge to pick up or set down passengers, but the tramways would not stop there. He suggested that further consideration should be given to the matter and that they should have a detailed report as to the total cost of the bridge and the purchase of property for the approaches of it. The MAYOR speaking in support of the committee's recommendation, said that some ol tla.s members seemed to be very much behindhand as regarded their informs- ' tion on the question. They had a report from Mr Webster a good many months ago in which the whole question was thoroughly discussed from an engineer's point of view and the report had been in the hands of the Council for a long time. He thought the time had now arrived when they should take some steps to deal with the report. He quite appreciated the fact that the question of incurring an expense o' £17,000 or £20,000 at the present time was a very serious matter, but the only thing which they ought to decide was the necessity for the expenditure. Everyone be thought including their friend Councillor Smethurst, would admit that the pre- sent bridge was inadequate for the traffic carried aver it. At any rate there was no difference of opinion when they approached the County Council and tried their very best to induce them to take part of the responsibility of providing for what they themselves said was a necessity caused by the present bridge being so narrow and inconvenient and wholly insufficient for the accommodation of the enor moos amount of traffic which had to cross thercover." That was the opinion of the County Cniacil and of the Corporation when it approached the County Council, The fact that the responsibility of providing the expen- diture necessary would now fall upon the Corperation instead of being divided between the Corporation and another authority, seemed to be not quite the sort of argument against the proposition which should appeal to business men. With regard to the waterway they I were entitled by an agreement with the Ship Canal Company to a sixty feet channel in the river which had to be dredged Owing to the narrow width of the central ' arch of the present bridge—the only part which could be used for the purpose of river truffle—they only got a channel of something like twenty feet, and Ihe thought that when they considered the condition of the river with a quick tide running, with probably only , twenty feet of channel, they would admit at once that it was not safe to navigate it and this acted as a strong bar ts the development of the upper portion of the river for the purposes of business. To his mind the most important argument in favour of the construction of , the bridge was that it was not a question of the width ' of Bridge-street, but the combined widths of all the I streets converging on the tridge, and which poured their traffic over the single inlet arid outlet of Warring-

ton. These was a belief that there was a growing disposition on the put of members of the Council not to take quite as keen an interest in a subject it it did not happen to effect the part of the town to whicto they belonged. Those unfortunate people who resided near the salubrious district cut In two by the Shit) Canal were frequently twitted with the fact that matters were brought forward to some." extent from a personal standpoint. He asked the Coun- cil to believe that those who resided in that district had I the interest of the town as a whole at heart, and not a ' particular district. Continuing, he said there would be a considerable increase of traffic when the tramways were put in operation. He knew from personal experi- ence that at present people preferred to walk rather than use the irregular and somewhat dangerous service of 'bus accommodation. Every member of the Council,' he tnought,was prepared to support the modified scheme of throwing out cantilevers. It was difficult to put on I paper the hotribly ugly appearance which cantilevers " attached to the bridge would hive. Trie serthetic point might not appeal to every member of the Council but he confessed it appealed to him and he should be sorry,' to see what was at present a beautiful bridge, distorted I beyond recognition by the addition of the cantilevers, I which had not added to the appearance of any town . where they had been put into existence. They were prepared, he understood,to spend g 3.300 on cantilevers in addition to the sum necessary tor purchasing land for the approaches. but if that scheme were adopted the bridge would be as ugly as it could he made and at the nr•ost could only accommodate the traffic for a few years. The repayment of the money in the time referred to wguld certainly amount to the repayment of the larger sum necessary for a new bridge spread over a longer period of years, so he failed to see where the economy came in. If they adopted the cantilever scheme they would be getting a mitigated improvement at precisely the same cost as they could get the larger improvement at once. A vote was then taken, and there voted— For the amendment Aldermen Monks and Elutchin- ' son, Councillors Smethurst, Illation, Davies, James Evans, Pierpoint, Burton, Plumpton, John Roberts. Forshaw, Peacock, Alfred Jolley,Duncan, Ellison, Hulse, and Tinnion (16). For the committee's recommendation : The Mayor, Aldermen Fairclough, Heston, and Bolton, Councillors Bennett, A J Jolley, Greening, Baird, John Evans, and Sampson (10).
„ The ameadment was therefore carried by 16 votes to 10.

div.head: WARRINGTON TRIP DAY. Messrs. Richmond's Employees at The Isle of Man. --- Presentation to Mr. H. E. Ransome.
div.p: WARRINGTON TRIP DAY. Messrs. Richmond's Employees at The Isle of Man. --- Presentation to Mr. H. E. Ransome.

Saturday's outing which was participated in by the Warrington employees of the Richmond Gas Stove and Meter Company, Limited, must be num- bered amongst the most successful ever held in connection with the firm. A variety of pleasant circumstances combined in making the event pass off most enjoyably, and not a single hitch occurred to mar the pleasure of the excursionists. That Queen of resorts—Douglas, was visited for the second year in succession and it seems not at all improbable that the Isle of Man will for some future years be the venue of Messrs Rich- mond's employees. The excursionists on Satur- day numbered over GOO, and they left War- rington for Liverpool in tnree special trains at 4.15, 4.25 and 4.30. For the passage to the Island, the steamship "King Orry "had been speci- ally chartered by the firm, and all the trippers having boarded her, the vessel left the Prince's landing stage at 5-30. Fortunately the weather conditions were all that could be desired, the sea was unusually calm, and the passage was safely accomplished in a little under five hours. It was just. 10.20 when the steamer reached Victoria Pier, and after the somewhat monotonous journey, the passengers were not sorry to reach terra firmz Once more. The firm had thoughtfully provided a capital breaufast for the trippers, four restaurants having been engaged to accommodate them. Needless to say, with appetites whetted by the long voyage, ample justice was done to the excellent fare pro- vided. After breakfas` the excursionists proceeded to Wellington Hall, Duke-street, where a short meeting, at which a very pleasing ceremony was performed, was held. Mr EW T Richmond, who was accompanied by Mr and Mrs Richmond, pre- sided, and he was supported on the platform by some of the directora andiheada of the firm. The prin- cipal object of the gathering was to make a presen- tation to Mr Liarolu E. Ransome, who has been connected with the firm as director and manager almost since its inception, but unfortunately, has been compelled to resign owing to ill-health. Abundant evidence of the esteem in which he has been held by the workpeople, was forthcoming on ISaturday, when Mr Ransome was the recipient of a purse containing sixty guineas and a beautiful framed illuminated address, expressive of the good feeling existing between himself and the em- ployees.

- Mr RICIDIOND, who was cordially received, said there were two matters about which he wished to speak to them, one being the presentation to their old friend and colleague Mr Harold Ransome, and the other, the opportunity which was to be afforded the workpeople of taking up some ordinary shares in the company. Fifteen or sixteen years ago be stood in that Hall to make one of his first speeches in relation to gas stoves and it would no doubt interest' them to know that on the present occasion he was addressing some of the men who were in the Hall when he spoke on the former occasion. At that time the firm held a gas ex- hibition in the Hall, and a very saccessful exhibition it was. Continuing Mr Richmond said be was glad that Father Neptune bad been kind to them, and allowed them to have a very pleasant voyage. He hoped he would be equally kind to them on the return journey, and that those who stayed at Douglas over the weelmind would have a very pleasant Sunday, and go hack feeling all the more ready to work next week. He was always pleased to attend those outings, for he felt !t was not only a duty but a very great pleasure to him to meet not only the men,but their wives and future wives.(Latuhter.)This outing was the 3econll they had had to the Isla of Man, and last year's was such an unfortunate one, that he felt very much concerned as to whether they would like to come again. He thought If they got weather like that they were now enjoying they would not hesitate about coming to the Isle of Man. (Hear.hear•) As regarded next 3 ear he thought it was rather trying for them to have to get up at 3 o'clock in order to catch trains, and he suggested that they might very well make the starting time about an hour and a half later. The trains would then leave Warrington at six o'clock and the boat would sail at seven o'clock, and instead of starting for home at seven,they could leave at 8 or 8.30.• Proceeding to speak of the prosperity of the firm he said that they kept getting stuff into stock and at this time of the year it rolled out as last as they could make it. (Applause.) They had therefore a great deal to be thankful for on that score. Mr Richmond then went on to mention the scrvices rendered to the firm by Mr Rarasome. He said that gentleman had been with them almost from the start. He was connected with the firm when they competed in a test at Nelson, against nearly all the other gas stove firms in the country. They then came out on top, and be (Mr Richmond) did the cooking. (Laughter.) Mr Ransome was one who helped them in those days to do what re- sulted in such success. He did his best and encouraged others to do the same. Unfortunately he was now un- able to work actively like he had done in the past. They very much appreciated all be had done, and the directors had shown their appreciation by providing for him in the future' Whilst h 3 knew Mr Ransoms appre- ciated that, vet he was sure that the manifestation of regard which he (Mr Richmond) was about to ark his acceptance of would be equally as acceptable to him as it came from those who had worked with him. Mr RicermoND then read the text of the illuminated address which was as follower—"On the;occasion of your resigning your appointment as a director and as general manager of our Warrington works, your co-directors and the Warrington employees, together with the entire staff of the company, desire to record their appreciation of your services and to express their regret and their sympathy with you upon your retirement. The opinion is unanimous throughout the concern that you have been one of the company's most capable officers and that you have combined shrewd and sagacious business aptitude with justness,kiradnesS, and consideration. The directors have shown their appreciation and sympathy by asking your acceptance of a retiring allowance, and as a practical token of the esteem in which you are held by those who have worked with you, a purse of guineas will be presented %long with this address. You have our sincere wishes for many years of happy usefulness in your new surroundings." Continuing Mr Richmond said the purse contained £69 6s, so be throoght it was a very substantial as well as sympathetic way of show- ing how much they appreciated Mr Ramsome when .be was with them. Re was sure from what he knew ot Mr Ransome that he would always have a very tender place in his heart for the employees of Richmord and Company 'when he looked at the address, and they were very glad to think that be would go away with such a pleasing and happy memento of the many useful years which he had spent with them. (Ap• plause.) In accepting the gifts Mr RANSOME said he thanked them all most sincerely for the very handsome present. He could assure them that the illuminated address would occupy a prominent position in the best room in his house, and that the I money would not be wasted. It was very nice to hear the kind remarks which Mr. Richmond had made and it was gratifying to know that such good feeling existed towards himself and his wife. He felt that his brother

was very oapable of taking the placS which be (the speaker) bad been so reluctantly compelled to leave. He thanked Mr Richmond with all his heart for the kind and sympathetic way in which he had alluded to his unfortunate illness.

Mr. Rica:imam then read two telegrams which be had received. One was from the Stratford employees and read " Stratford heartily wish you a most enjoyable day at Douglas." The other was from the Dublin works and was as follows:—" Best wishes for an enjoyable day and flue weather from the Dublin lads." Continuing Mr Richmond said they;all knew the way in which the profit sharing echeme had been carried on for four or five years at Warrington and Stratford. Last year the firm corn- menced negotiations to purchase the meter business of George Glover and Company, Chelsea. The arrange meats were completed this year, and now not only did tries manufacture gas stoves but also meters, and in addition to manufacturing them they had been selling them very quickly. (Applause). Of course, when they purchased a business they had to issue capital shares to pay for it. They issued shares and paid for the busi- ness,but now that the otdinary shares were being issued a large number of employees asked if they could not:take some of them. The shares which had up to now been given to the employees were the preference capital sharee They bad bad £1 shares which brourit in 6 per cent. interest. Before any part of the profit went to the' ordinary shareholders, those holding preference shelve had to be paid their share of the profits ; but they bad n 3 claim upon anything else. The ordinary share- holders took all the profit which was left after the pre- ference capital had been paid. The result was that when the concern was doing well the ordinary :shares were worth double as much as the preference shares, but if the firm did badly they would not be worth as much. Last year the firm did better than ever and , paid in percent. on ordinary shares. He brought for- I ward the matter of allowing the employees to take ordinary shares,at a Board meeting and they had decided that everyone in the employ of the concern, whom they were satisfied did their best for the company, should be allowed to subscribe for Bharat up to one half of their annual salary. Those shares which would be offered to them for a guinea were to- day worth 38s; they were quoted at that on the Birming- ham stock exchange.' The directors had arranged that they could all take up the shares by paying down 2s for every E 1 share they wanted, and Is a week afterwards until the whole amount was paid. The £1 share would bring in 121 per cent, so long as the firm paid the same dividend as last year. They were giving them a ereat boon in this offer. It was the finest thing ever offered by any firm in Warrington, and he should think one of the finest things offered anywhere. The conditions were that they must not sell the shares for five years, and that if ttsey left the employ of the firm before five years had elapsed, the firm would have the right to take the shares at the price they (the work people) paid for them. It was expected that the cost to the firm would be repaid by the extra work the work- men would put into the business. The result of rhe arrangement would be that in time—it might be yeare —the employees would gradually become the share- holders entirely of Richmond and Company. They muse bear in mind that for every stove they made they were going to receive some profit. They might rely upon IS that if the scheme met with the success which was anti- cipated, other firms would follow their example. (Applause.) _ _ _
• , On the motion of Mr A Ransom!, seconded by Mr Hughes, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr, Mrs and Miss Richmond, and the proceedings terminated.

The excursionists were free to spend the remainder Of the day according to their inclinations. Many went by electric tram to the neighbouring resorts of Laxey• Groudle,and the various beautiful glens which are to be found on the island. Others ascended Douglas Dead, and enjoyed the fine views to be obtained from tbl,l eminence. The return journey was commenced at o'clock, Liverpool being reached shortly after 12 and Warrington at 1 30, It was generally agreed that the excursion had been one of the most enjoyable ever held.

div.head: WARRINGTON WALKING
div.p: WARRINGTON WALKING
DAY.
THE PROCESSIONS.

The glorious weather of Friday crowned the Walking Day Festival with unqualified success. During the whole day there were no dread symp- toms of inclemency to be seen in the skies, for the warm sun which rose upon the town early in the morning continued to shower down its welcome rays until the evening. ' So early as eight o'clock in the morning the town was astir with prattling youngsters, looking very dainty and pleasing in their new clothes. This subject of dress is one which calls:forth the thoughtfulness and willing assistance of the parents. The beautiful dresses which were to be seen in such great profusion yesterday could not be possible without the expenditure of a large amount of hard I cash, which in many cases involves much self- I sacrifice on the part of the parents. They are rewarded to some extent by witnessing the living wealth of colour and beauty as it traverses the streets on Walking Day and in the expressions of happiness so apparent on the faces of,the chiliren. To the scholars Walking Day is the day of days,and Friday's festival was more successful 4 perhaps, than any of its predecessors. Warrington wore its annual festive appearance and once more looked at ite best. Flags and ban- ners were to be seen protruding from windows and the whole length of the line of procession was be- decked with bunting. Here and there lines of flags, stretching across the street fluttered gaily in the gentle breeze. By nine o'clock the public began to assemble along th 3 line of the route of the pro- cession whilst others took up positions at windows from which a good view of the processions could be obtained. As the scholars walked along the streets in what appeared an endless chain, with pretty dresses and smiling faces, to-the strains of lively music and with banners floating overhead.the effect was pleasing to a degree. One of the prettiest sights was that witnessed from the Town Hall steps. From this elevated position a good view was ob- tained of the schools as they entered and left the Park. The assembly on the lawn was a picturesque spectacle. Detailed decorative effects were less easily attained in so vast a throng but the eye was attracted by many pretty spots of colour. In the mass, the display was imposing and quite up to the reputation of previous years. The tountaiu stand- ing almost in the centre of the throng, with its cooling sprays playing in the sunlight, gave an added attractiveness to the .spectacle. The Nonconformists, as in former years, did not organise a combined procession. There were, bow- ever,processions of numerous Nonconformist schools early in the morning. A few proceeded to the lawn in front of the Town Hall, but most of them left the town for pleasant spots in the immediate neighbourhood. F i or nstance.,tlae Wycliffe scholars entrained at Bank Quay Station for Dunham Hill, Bold-street Weslesrans journeyed to Lymm, whilst their friends at Silver-street school spent the day as Frodsbara. Southport Was visited by the Welsh Calvanist Methodist, and Frodsham was selected by the St John's Presbyterians. The Cairo-street congregation proceeded to Higher Walton to the grounds of Mr F Monks, and Walton Lea was again the rendezvous ef the Workingmen'e Mission. The scholars commenced to arrive on the lawn about half-pest nine and they were marshalled into position by Mr B T Fairclough and Mr J Craik,who have filled the onerous position of marshalls for a number of years. Perfect order was kept by Chief Inspector Phillips and a staff of police who showed a thorough understanding of their duties. By ten o'clock all the Church of England schools and Iseveral Nonconformist schools had arrived on the lawn and they were welcomed by the Mayor and a number of leading townspeople. Promptly at ten lo'clock, the signal was given for the first school to I move off. It was computed that at this moment 8,400 children were assembled on the lawn. The I Blue Coat School occupied the place of honour and headed by their own band the children connected 1 with this ancient Warrington charity filed through the central arch. All the banners carried were entirely new. The incriptions were the same, the one in the forefront indicating that the charity was founded in 1677. Another banner bore the in- scription" Fear God; honour the King." The old banners which were yesterday discarded for new had been carried in the procession such year since 1862. The usual route was taken and the arrange- ments for lassies to rejoin the procession were the same as in previous years. These heavy and sub- stantial vehicles drawn oy horses, decorated with ribbons and bells, and conveying their human freight of smiling youngsters were taken down the western drive and rejoined their respective schools as the piocession of scholars proceeded on its way down Arpley-street. All the lurries had been more or less decorated and some pretty effects were pro- duced. One lurry contained a number of St Peter's infants all dressed in spotless sailor suits, and was quite a centre of attraction. The following was the order in which the, schools left the park : I. Blue Coat School and Band. 2 Padgate Industrial Schools and Band. 3. Parish Church and Hollinfare Schools and Walton Band. 4. St George's Mission and Lvmm Band. 5 St Clement's Mission and Church Lads Brigade
Buzle Band. 6. St Paul's and Band. 7. All Saints Mission. 8. Holy Trinity and Preston Brook Band. 9. Factory-yard. Mission.

10. St. Luke' School. 11. St. Janes' and the Volunteer Brass Band. 12. St. Ann's and Walker's Band. 13. St Barnabas and Fletcher'a Band. 14 St. Peter's and "Guardian" Band. 15 Emmanuel and Reformed Church. 16. Legh-street Primitive Methodists and own
17. Latchford Primitive Methodists. 18 Shape-street Primitive Methodist. 19. Buckley-street Independent Methodist and

own Band. 20. Salvation Army and Band. 21. Raggen School and Band. 22, Sankey Bridges Wesleyans and Monks Band Very few special features were introduced by any of the schools, and as a result the procession was much the same as in previous years. Here and there a new banner could be descried. Some. of the banners ware tastetul and expressive; others redeemed crudity of design by an excellent moral purpose. Floral crowns were displayed on the top of poles and suspended from them were coloured ribbons held by charming little fairies rejoicing in their beauty and attire. Others carried bunches of marguerites whilst a number carried pretty baskets filled with beautiful flowers. Decora- ted mail carts were again much to the fore and pretty children were to 'tie seen cosily ensconced under canopies of bright material. Prominence was given to the Christian Enieavour movement in the Emmanuel Reformed Church procession. Near the front was an artistically worked mono- gram "C E" and a banner bore the motto of the Christian Endeavour Society " For Christ and the Church." In connection with the Parish , Church and St Peter's, the Church Lads Brigade was prominent in the proc ssion, the lads shouldering their guns onl marching in soldierly style. As the long procession neared its end one could not but contrast the petty co Itumes of the scholars who had gone before with those worn by the boys and girls in the procession of the Salva- tion Army and Ragged school, who brought up the rear. Here were boys and girls srom the poorer dis• tricts carrying their drinking cans,in charge of the faithful lasses with pokey bonnets and other teachers and friends. DeSpil'el the pove-ty of many ,of the children they were for the nonce heartily I enjoying themselves and proudly carried aloft the Union Jacks which had been so plentifully dis- tributed. Aft,er proceeding along the appointed route the scholars attended service at their respective churches In the afternoon they adjourned to fields where they disported themselves right merrily.

- - The Roman Catholic Procession. A Charming Spectacle It was generally conceded that the procession of Roman Catholic scholars, which commenced soon after the Church of Englaqd procession had trav- ersed the fixed route, was one of the most charming and picturesque spectacles ever seen in Warring- ton. Of course, for originality and beautiful effect, the palm has always by common consent, been awaroed to th 3 Roman Catholic,, but .Friday's display completely surpassed all previous efforts. This is saying a great deal,as no doubt all who bare been accustomed to witnessing the processions of former years will agree, but it is nevertheless a fact which will be endorsed hy all who saw Friday's pageant, F.,r many weeks

past the work of preparation for the great event had been in progress, but the efforts of those who had undertaken the duties attendant upon the organization of such a brilliant exhibition as that seen yesterday mew have been amply repaid by the warm eulogiums showered upon them by the thousands of spectators who thronged the line of route. The most complete arrangements to ensure the successful carrying out of the proces- .ion had been made and the whole proceedings dassed off without the slightest hitch. The start- ing point of the combined procession was Bridge Foot, and having been formed into line the scholars from the five schools wended their way thither. By the time the pageant left Bridge Foot, Bridge- street was densely crowded with eager spectators. Some difficulty was experienced in clearing suffi- cient open space for the processionists, and the task of the police officers upon whom this duty de- volved, was not an enviable one. It was about a quarter to twelve when the music of an approach- ing band was heard, and the scholars comprising the first portion of the procession—those of St Mary's,Latchford,—were seen slowly making their way over Warrington Bridge. In a few minutes the procession came into Al view, headed by the Run.. 1 corn St Edwards Baud, and a beautiful banner. A number of gentlemen of the congregation followed, and afterwards came more banners. As in former years the banners were a prominent feature of the Roman Catholic procession. They were of fine texturei and workmanship, and on them were de- picted the deeds of Saints and also the Seven Sacra- ments of the church, The flowing ribbons of various tints attached to them, were carried by prettily attired girls. After a number of banners had passed, the school children of St. Mary's came linto view, and they made a charming picture. The Confraternities of the Sacred Heart and Children of 'Mary concluded the St. Mary's, Latchford, proces- sion. The next school to appear was the Sacred Heart, Bank Quay, and they made an extremely creditable display. A special feature was. the introduction of a number of girls dressed in beauti- ful Italian costumes with jingling tambourines. 'Messrs Crosfield's band supplied the music for this part, of the procession. The combined schools of St Alban's and St Benedict's now appeared, and it may safely be said that their display constituted the most attractive part of the whole pageant. A glittering processional cross was the first object to arrest the attention of the onlooker, and behind it, followed acolytes and altar boys in cassocks and surplices, several gentlemen of the congregation, the members of the Catholic Association, and the beautiful banner of St Bane- des. The Orford-lane children were headed by the Borough Band, who appeared for the first time in their splendid new uniform, which,by the way,was made entirely by a local firm The confraternity of the children of Mary made a very imposing feature. Tney were proceeded by a statue of the Blessed Virgin, which was exquisitely decorated with choice flowers and trailing creepers, and this was undoubtedly the centre piece of the procession. Father Nugent's Refuge Band was once more en evidence and considering the youthfulness of the performers, showed remarkable proficiency. The infants of St. Benedict's are deserving of special mention For uniformity, delicate taste, and artistic display, as welt as perfect grouping, it would be difficult to excel this part of the procession and the Misses O'Connell and Fitzpatrick who were responsible for the arrange- ments must be congratulated on the splendid success of their jsint efforts, Some 300 children represented this school and they marched in Indian file—the boys on one side the girls on the other—leaving ample space for the exquisite floral devices carried between. Dressed alike in white with pale blue sashes, the boys wore tiny caps to match edged with gold lace, while the girls wore dainty wreaths in their hair. All carried gilt crosses decked with rose bouquets, and a pleasing feature was the merry tinkle of:musical bells affixed to the little shoes, which served to bring into prominency the perfect marchinz time. Between the rows of children a beautitully decorated shield bearing the name of the school was carried, A magnificent floral arch borne by four young ladies, and surrounded by eight little ones holding delicate blue streamers gave a grand effect to the whole. The arch was composed of ferns and green trailing plants picked out with violets and pink roses, A splendid cross of similar design, but with tea roses gave if possible a grander and nobler tone to the picture. The piece de resistance however, was a lovely, harp of ferns and greenery set off by pink roses with streamers of green and gold. The last school in the pageant was St. Mary's, Butter- market-street, and their display t 00, surpassed al previous attempts. The infants, in this C3BO were the premier attraction, their get-up being most effective. The banners of the Seven Sacraments formed an inter- esting portion of this school's exhibition. The Band of the League of the Cross and the Junior Fife Band supplied the music. Altogether, the display was a magnificent one, and well merited the encomiums bestowed upon it. It may be mentioned that over 3,000 persons took part in the procession, including 700 members of the various confraternities. The route traversed was as follows • —Bridge-street, Horsemarket-street, Bewsey-street, Edgeworth-street, Legh-street, Bath street, past the Town Hall, and along Sankey-street to Market Gate. The Schools separated at Market Gate, and the children proceeded to their respective churches, webere there was the Benediction of the Blessed Sacram, tat. A large field in Padgate-lane, belong'ng to Mr Bennett, had been secured by St Alban's and St Mary's schools, for the holding of the afternoon and evening festivities. Owing to the glorious weather which prevailed it is calculated that abut 10,000 persons in addition to the scholars visited the field during the course of the day. A host of amusements was provided and a most enjoyable time was spent.

Authors of letters intended for publication must I in all cases send their names and addresses to the Editor. Correspondents are strongly advised to write briefly. A short letter has much greater chance of insertion than a long one. We cannot under ordinary circumstances under- take to return the manuscripts which are not used. , 171 The Queen's Hall Meeting. Sir,—When I read your paragraph in last Saturday's ' Examiner " about the above meeting in London, I thought it must have been meant for one of the daily jiugo papers and not for the columns of the Liberal "Examiner." Your description of the meeting was ai much coloured by blind prejadice as it was grossly Inaccurate. The meeting was organised and supported by men whose record as Liberals and as honourable men, is not second to that of any in the party. Such members of Parliament as Lloyd George, T Burt, J Burns, Broadhurst, T B Roberts, C P Scott, Charming, Cremer, Bell, Pease, Szc &c., and such men as Allan Bright, Sir Wilfred Lawson, Dr Clifford, Passmore Edwards. F Maddison, Joshua Rowntree,Frederic Harri son, Page Hoppe, and Silas Hocking &c. ko., a class of men who are the backbone of the Liberal party. It is quite plain from the terms of your description, the class of paper you got your information from. The stewards were" Chuckers out "and about 700 of them. John Burns' honourable constituents from Battersea were "Hooligans." You seem not to have been aware that anonymous circulars had been distributed for days previously at Lloyds and on the Exchange urging violent opposition to the meeting and that the jingo press of London hail dot* likewise. But for standing up for free epeech like Britons, you call the defenders of the meeting " Hooligans." You sneer at its being called a public meeting because a number of tickets (not one third) were issued, yet half an hour before the commencement the doors were thrown open to the public, yet you say nobody was admitted but by ticket ! You consider it a griev- ance that one or two raw students, who began to in- terrupt the proceedings ere expelled, as would be the case if some raw young Tories were to attempt to interrupt a Liberal meeting at Warrington. But Mr Chamberlain's doctrine that any man who dares to express an opinion that the war is a needless and I wicked war, is a traitor to his country and is to be treated with sneers and illusage—seems rather to find favour in quarters where it should be indignantly I repudiated. You say the supporters asked the Govern- ment to "sue for peace." What they did ask was that the Government should do justice and treat the Boers who have as much right to fight for what they believe to be their riglcts as Englishmen have,with the considera- tion due to a race as brave and stubborn as ourselves. You say the opponents of the war have a right to their opinions but no right to give public expression to them which means that we must yield " with bated breath and whispering humbleness" to your superior wisdom. But we are not made of that kind of stuff. I fear you have like many others mistaken popular feeling,misled by designing men for popular wisdom. Have you forgotten how some century ago a mad King led a mad nation to go to war with the North American Colonies. Then as now the nation was wild for the war, and in spite of the eloquent opposition of Chatham. Burke and Fox the greatest statesmen of that time, Parliament declared in its favour just as now, by a majority of more than two to one. We assailed the farmer colonists with all the lying abuse that could be invented almost in the very language we have used to the Boers since the war began. Yet we failed to coerce those simple farmer Colonists, and they got the independence they so nobly fought and suffered for. The result is the rise of a nation, our most formidable rivals in trade and commerce tc-day. What I most object to in this con- troversy is that you don't attempt to answer our arguments, but give us ill names and abuse. For 50 years I I have worked for the Liberal party in my native town and one of my dearest hopes has been for the success of its grand principles. but I fear that this bastard Imperialism has thrown it back for many years. As for the attitude of the Christian churches gener- ally with some noble exceptions, I dare not trust m7self to speak. By its silence in this financial war between Christian nations it stands condemned, In the words of one of the Bishops it has "had no message from the Lord " during this terribly expressed determination to crush out of exist- ence men whom we profess to believe are equally with ourselves be children of God and brothers in the great human family. It has been painful to me to write I this letter, and to blame where I would rather praise but I felt it incumbnit on me not to let your paragraph pass without protest. Yours &c. T. BIRCHALL.

div.head: EARLESTOWN & N EWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN & N EWTON.
THEFT FROM A SHOP AT GOLBORNE.-BOY RECEIVES THE BIRCH.

At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednesday, before lmeBsre G Comber (in the chair) and J Ball, Thomas Cassidy, a boy, was charged with stealing two shillings in silver and a quantity of chocolate cream, the property of John Arrow- smith, who r keeps a shop at 41, Bank-street, Golborne.—Mrs Arrovsmith stated that on the afternoon of June 22nd she left the shop for half an hour. On returning she found the back door open and on looking in the shop window found a quantity of chocolate was missing. Subsequently she missed 28 in silver from the cupboard.—P.C. Johnson stated he apprehended the prisoner, who admitted steal- ing 2, and two bars of chocolate.—P.S. Young said he had known the prisoner six years. and he had been a very had boy during the whole of that time. He had been constantly pilfering and had been convicted once for theft at Newton.—lt was stated that the boy was remanded at Newton last week with a view to his being sent to a school. It had been ascertained that there was a vacancy at Birk- I dale Farm Echool.—Prisoner's father pleaded hard for him not to be sent away, and the magistrates sentenced the boy to twelve strokes with the birch.
The great fire which broke out at Eluntingdnn West, Virginia, U S A , on Tuesday destroyed two entire Equates in the centre of the city, It was at first feared tbat the whole town would be wiped out.

div.head: EXAMINER FRIDAY, JULY 5, 1901
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY, JULY 5, 1901

the two races, fomented by a press owned by the great capitalists, and by a variety of political leagues whose avowed object was to bring all this irritation to a decisive issue. This was unquestinnably an ugly situa- tion which called for a remedy. About that we are all agreed. But is the soar any real remedy or the beet remedy for such a case. The question at issue is (1) whether , the war which we have been waging is likely to bring 1 any improvement about, and (2) whether it has not in itself created evils which no conceivable political gain can ever outweigh. When Sir Alfred Milner called for " extreme measures," when Mr Chamberlain made violent speeches that could only lead to war, when our Government called out the reserves and announced that it was preparing an ultimatum,it w asacting on a theory which events have falsified. It calculated that the war would be short, cheap and glorious. The official esti- mate of its cost during the autumn session of 1899 was ten millions. We began by sending first 20,000, then 35,000 troops to the front. Their Cimrnander-in-Chief announced that h 3 would eat his Christmas dinner in Pretoria. Finally it was said that the Boers would welcome a change of flag, that they would respect us for heating them, that a conclusive demonstration of our power was all that was needed to reconcile the two races and inaugurate an era of happiness and peace. Now if all these calculations had been accurate,the war would have been not a whit 'sore just indeed, but cer- tainly it would not have c 'used such frightful inischief. We can now cleat our minds of these miscalculations. Let us wk ourselves whether We should have gone to war in October 1399 had we then posessed the know- ledge which we have gained by June, 1901. WHAT SHALL WE GAIN?

In the first place, what shall— we gain ? The gold- fields ? The goldfields belong to a small group of cosmopolitan financiers, for the most part German and French Jews. They indeed reckoned that the war would add ai millions to their yearly profits, That would not have benefitted us. The Territory ? We shall be lucky if we escape running the territory at a dead loss. Sir David Barbour has now made his official rsport on the finances of the Republics. In the Free State he anticipates a more or less constant deficit. Any small Surplus from the Transvaal will be more than swallowed up by the cost of General Baden-Powell's Special Con- stabulary, which, it is estimated, will reach £2,500,000 per annum. Add to this the cost of the large garrison which we shall have to keep in South Africa to coerce the Dutch. We have had to increase our Army, and ovsr and above all this we have still to pay. off the cost of the war—at least £150,000,000. Clearly there is .01; much prospect of gain here. From the financial point of view it is very bad business, but will the politieal situation be better ? We complained that Mr Kruger's franchise was too narrow. Mr Chamberlain's proposal is to govern the Renublics as Crown Colonies. There will be no repre- sentative institutions at all. There will be no juries, The magistrates will be removable at the will ot Lord Milner. That is the present programme and this state of things will last, says Lord Salisbury, "for years or it may be for generations." The Transvaal, it was said, was an "obligarchy." We are setting up an autocracy in its place under the very man whom the Dutch most detest and dislike. The Free State was by general admission a model commonwealth. We have swept away its whole fabric of liberty end progress. There is little prospect of gain here. Will the mass of the Eit- landers be better off? Already they are complaining bitterly that the new British bureacracy in the Trans vaal has been captured by the capitalists. Almost every office has so far been given to men who are or who were in the pay of the great financial houses. THE TWO RACES• And finally how will the relations of the two races stand? The Colonial English are not more charitable or more kindly because of the life and death struggle that has been waged. The Dutch do not respect us because WP may eventually succeed in beating to their knees the 17,000 farmers still in arms against us. They will not love is for attempting to enforce"unconditional surrender" and to rob them of "every shred of their independence." The Dutch after all are men of like passions with ourselves. They are apt to resent an injury and to cherish the memory of a wrong. And what memory will they retain of this war when it does come to an end ? Some of them have perhaps received kindnesses from individual offilers and soldiers—for our soldiers have been more merciful than our politicians, more generous than our newspapers. But this conuot alter the things that have been done in our name. We have devastated with fire and sword two c luotries that once were prosperous and happy. As the recent return of farm-burning shows, whole districts have b,en ''laid waste." We have blown up their mills, destroyed their farm implements, swept up their sheep and their cattle, and burned their crops. Those whom we captured we have kept in dismal confinement in the hottest stations of the tropics—Bombay, Ceylon, St Helena. When they return they will find that their homes have been ruined, and their household goods have venial:Led, while their cattle, their chief wealth,have been eonfiscated. When ever the owner (after September 1900) was still on corn mando, ru in will stare them in the face. Old me will have to begin life anew, and young men who had prospects, wII find themselves paupers in a beggared land. But worst of all are there Concentration Camps. Wnen we burned the farms and " denuded " the country we also " c oncentrated " the women and children in prison camps. The facts about these have be:n described for us by Miss Hobhou le and Mr ROwntree. I will recall a few of them. Fur some months the women whose hustands or sons were still fighting against us were k Tit on half rations. We held them all. close prisoners of war within barbed wire fences, whilspentries with fixed bayonets mounted guard. It ca n Hippened that mothers, separated from their little children, attempted to escape. They were recaptured and punished. For the children we provided —perhaps we could provide—no s aitable food. Young babies had to make shift with bully beef and meshes. The water providol was frequently a mere solution of typhoid germs. Is the summer delicate women slakened In the beat of an aVer•crowded tent. In the winter mothers expecting their confinement lay on the wet ground without so much as a mattress. New born babies saw the world under a thin Canvas, through which the rain soaked and pawed. The result has been a mortality which the med meal plague could hardly have rivalled. 'The children have died like flies on the Molt frosty day in autumn. In our towns at home the death-rate per thousand per annum averages 22 In the Johannesburg Camp it W4l during May 435. In the Bloemfontein Camp it was 383. These figures are more lent than ans. de3cription. This is the tale—a tale of woe—the Boer prisoners will hear when they return from Ceylon and Bombay. Fathers will learn that the war has killed their children, brothers will miss their 'sisters, husbands; vow to avenge their wives. A burnt farm and a dead child are not the best foundation on which to build an era of peace and reconciliation. WAS IT NECESSARY ?

WO are told, of course, that all this suffering is neces- sary and inevitable. Tbe same argument was used %viten the hospital scandals were exposed. It was said that War is war and you cannot avoid inflicting suffer- ing on the enemy and pain and disease on your own soldiers. Well, if that is so it is only a fresh argument against war. If it was inevitable that our men shou:d be on wet grouod at Bloemfontein in crowded tents suffering from typhoid without milk, without medicines without nurses, then we ouzht to be more cautious abut going to war. We ought to hare striven harder to avoid it. And the same is true about the women'a camps. War is always terrible, but it is doubly so if your medical deportment breaks down and your War Office is hampered with red tape. But after all were , the camps Inevitable? We had of course to do something to keep the women from starving when oncr3 we had burned their farms. But nay burn their farms at all. It was done to shorten the war. It has had precisely the opposite effect. It has turned the Boers into des- 'aerate men. They had nothing more to lose. We have destroyed their stake in tho country, and an outlaw will fight m. when a farmer would surrender. More- over such a policy as this does not dispose the Boers to trust ull• We ask them to place their whole fat 3 in our bands without reserve. Are they more likely to have an implicit confidence in us after we have destroyed their homes and deported their families ? But even if we grant that the camps were necessary, was it necessary to put the wives of the fighting burghers on half rations? Was it necessary to ref use the women permission to join their friends In Cape Colony ? Was the failure to provide nurses and mattresses and suitable food for the coildrea necessary ? To all these questions there is the best of all possible answers. Mr Broderick has now promised ta alter the system in all these particulars. If that decision had been taken six months ago, the greater part of this misery might have been avoided. But after all the real fault has been an insistence on unconditional surrender. Sir Redvers Buller would have offered terms to the B 3ers last June. Lord Kitchener would have granted them ' representative government in April. The soldiers have always been more generous than the politicians. It is the Government which has prolonged the war and the government which dictated a policy that has carried so many horrors in its train. THE POLICY, THE RESULTS, THE EXCUSES. Such are the consequences of this war to the Orange River Colony and the Transvaal. What has it done for us ? -It has hro9glit us no military glory, we have lost , thousands upon thousands oft be flower of our manhood. I Our finance. are embarrassed. We have earned the ' anger and the contempt of the civilized world. This war has inaugurated an era of repression and coercion in South Africa.lt has taught the Dutch—a formidable race with a long memory—to hate us With a personal and an individual hate. It has loaded innocent women and young children with degradation, wretchedness and pitiful physical suffering. If these are the consequences of the war, surely some v,ry stern necessity, some very plain and inexorable logic of facts are needed to justify it. The onus of proof rests with those who, if they did not sigh for war (and only too many did), at least took no precautions to avoid it • above all with those whose provocative speeches and diplomacy invited it. Nor will it be sufficient to refer to the loyalty of the colonies, the patriotism of our own people, the courage and chivalrF of -,:r :okliers and the stamina of the raca of which thi. ac has given proof. Who doubted them?

div.head: Naphtha Ship Blown up.
div.p: Naphtha Ship Blown up.
Loss of Seven Lives.

The Danish schooner Anna, laden with naphtha. had been blown up while oassing,through the Catte- gat. The naphtha, from some unexplained cause, ignind, and the vessel was shattered by the vio- lence of the subsequent explosion. Seven of the crew perished either by drowning or burning. Only one man was saved.

div.head: Death of Professor Tait.
div.p: Death of Professor Tait.

Prefessor Tait, of Edinburgh University, died in Edinburgh yesterday morning. Since the death of his son, Lieutenant Tait, the golf champion, in South Africa, the deceased has been in indifferent health.

div.head: WAR. By Mr. ArtWL7FI. Crosfield.
div.p: THE WAR. By Mr. ArtWL7FI. Crosfield.
ARTICLE I.

To review the origin of a war that is already nearing the end of its second year, and to weigh the apologies that have been offered for a policy which a majority in the country has ratified may seem at first sight to be labour wasted. But these questions are after all germane to the practical issue before us Our views on the settlement must to some extent depend on our views about the dip- lomacy which preceded the war. If the war was just and inevitable then undoubtedly the Boers are entitled to much less consideration than we ought to grant them if we come to the conclusion that the main burden of responsibility for this de- plorable conflict rests upon the authors of the Jameson raid. At present we are not fighting to bring about reforms, nor even to break the armed power of the Transvaal, but to beat the Boers to their knees—till, in fact, they are forced to accept whatever terms we impose. That is a hard fate to inflict upon a whole people. Whatever Mr Kruger's faults may have been—and they were many—we must not forget that tire men now at the head of the fighting Boers were in no way responsible for his foolish and reactionary attitude. General Botha his always been a progres•ive, and Christian De Wet bitterly opposed the war. If they are irreconcileable to-day the fault lies with our Government which sanctioned the policy of farm- burning and determined to insist on unconditional surrender. Most of us had hoped that those Liberals who came to the conclusion that the war was necessary and justifiable would by now have been with us in insisting that terms should, even at the eleventh boor, be offered the Men which there is some chance of their acmpting—against the grain it may be—as a condition of peace. One can hardly believe that a Liberal like Mr Asquith, for whom we all feel the greatest respect and regard, will tolerate a policy of fighting to the bitter end, unless it is fist ma le clear that terms have been offered which the Boors might wittout dishonour accept. The views of men like Mr Asquith and Sir Edward Gray, to whom we all look for great things in the future,dsserve a candid and dispassionate consideration. Liberals should differ as men who hope to be re-united at no distant day—re-united to work out a programme as far- reaching in its influence on the general welfare of the nation as any programme of reform which has preceded it. At the same time it is per- haps not unfair to suggest that both Mr Asquith and Sir Edward Grey are very naturally biassed by their long-standing and intimate friendship with Lord Milner. He has been a chief actor in all this tragic drama, and that fact alone must make it difficult for his friends to main- tain a really impartial attitude. This personal factor, however, should only encourage our hop that these differences between Liberals will be merely temporary. They are largely accidental and flow from no fundamental divergence about political principles. In Warrington, at any rate, we look for entire reunion. Let us hope for the most part it will be the same in the country. If indeed there are a few who will find in this critical time an opportunity for changing their political creed—some I few who the moment they feel their feet planted on , the Social platform set to work to kick down every I one of the ladders by which they climbed there— vv,,, shall not be alarmed. They will not be the first in history or the last to play this little game,aud we may pass them by in silence. But for unworthy insinuations which have been made, iti hould be unnecessary to add that if:some of the methods involved in the Government's policy stand condemned in public opinion no reflection whatever is thereby ca-t upon our soldiers. Very much tin reverse; for they have helped to mitigate ' the severity of the.t policy, and letters which have appeared in the press go to show that our men have carried out the work of farm-burning with disgu4t and reluctance. As for the "refugee" camps the, Boer women are only suffering from the same , neglect which made our own military hospitals a ' scandal and a disgrace. As Mr Rowntree has told us. our private soldiers have often stinted them- selves to relieve the hunger of our women captives. That will redound to their lasting credit,but it does not exculpate the system!, or lessen the Govern- ment's responsibility for it. I have no claim to write, nor will I pretend for one moment to write from the standpoint of the unco' guid ; but if there is one maxim which, more than any other, goes to the root of all Liberalism it, is John Locke's oft-quoted aphorism that the end of Government is the good of Mankind. Will our South Afr'can policy square with this'? FULLER KNOWLEDGE.

We are, after all, in a better position to-day to debit,. the question whether the war was justifiable, than we were in October, 1899. We were then engt gecl in a dis. putt" of long standing with the Boers. On ii,irne counts we had, as all parties agreed, a fairly strong ease. I, is a ludicrous fiction to ray that the Outlanders on whose behalf we i ltervened were" rppresaecl " lfltheorOjcjry sense of the word. It is doubtful whether mans, of them really wanted the franchise which became the bone of contention. Hut certainly fTr. • Brugeirs ad- ministration wrs a Tory Government of a decidedly reactionary type. The system of indirect taxa- tion was prinaitive, and the ex(cutive had probably, in some of its branches succumbed to the bribes of the corrupt gold magnates. The lei] trouble, however, was the perpetual friction between

As Mr Carnegie in effect observed the other day (in his memorab:e article in the " Nineteenth Century ") no limits can be placed to the patriotism, loyatty and invincible cJura,e which will be shown by British people if ever the Empire is imperilled. We did not need an evil and disastrous war to prove this. Then what are the reasons given for this policy ? With your Ilind permission, sir, I propose to examine them in another le'ter. If you will allow me to do so, I will endeavour to summarise and examine them as fairly and dispassionately as may be possible for a mere party man. It should be possible even for him to discuss with some impartiality a qutstion the national and Imperial importance of which so completely outweighs any tem- porary effect it may have on the interests of any party, Whig or Tory.
