Messrs J Mclntyre, W Turner, T Wright, J Stokes, C E Linaker. P G:eave, T Lewis.l Moun field, Gt-trge Pilling. T Btx ter, J Clarke, J Miseley Wiihams, J B Chadwick, James Edwards. W Ellison, with Messrs Ge-enre f, Ashton (clerk),4W E Hough (assistant clerk), Mr J Ftrrington (lispector), Messrs J Swinton and W Diggle (survey- ors), and Dr J Adams (madical officer.)
A PROTEST FROM STOCKTON HEATH.

Mr Noel T. Kershaw, assistant aecretary, Lo &I Government Board wrote under date 18:h June: Sir,—l arn directed by the Local Government Board to advert to your letter of the 15th alt, and to request that they may be furnished with the observations of the Rural District Council of Runcorn upon the enclosed copy of letters which the board have received from Joseph Clarke of Hearhfield,Stockton Heath, and Messrs Spencer Wallhead and Son of Warrineton. The following are conies of the letters referred re : Heathfield, Stockton Heath, Cheshire 13th May, 1901. The Secretary, Local Government Board, London, sir, —Stockton Heath Parochial Committee. At a meeting of this committee (of woich lam a member) held on the 2nd inst., a resolution was proposed by Mr. George Pilling, district councillor of Latchford Without, and supperte be Mr Joseph Knowles, district councillor of Appleton, and carnal hy the votes of these two gen- tlemen, that the sum of £lO he paid to Mr. S winton,the district surveyor of the Runcorn D:strict Council, for increased work on account of numerous buildings being erected in this parish, and for attending the monthly meetings of the Committee. Th, same to be a charge on the special rate of the parish. I beg to ask you if yen consider this a legal and right charge C.., be put on this parish solely ? I opposed the resolution but was out- voted by the votes of the two mentioned district coun- cillors. My reasons for objecting are :—(1) That the work the Surveyor performs comes within the ordinary routine of his duties, and if these duties increase any advance in his salary should he chargeable to the whole Union, and not to a specific parish where his laboura may happen to be a little heavier. (2) It appears to be unfair that district councillors from outlying parithei should have the power to attend our meetings and pro- pose money payments which are chargeable solely on our special rate. I understand this proposition will require the sanction of your Board, and I trust that considering the circumstances under which it was I carried. your Board will see its way to withhold its con- sent.—! am, sir, your obedient servant, JO 3EPII H. CLARKE.

Warrington, 3rd June, 1901. To the Local Govern- meat Board, London. Gentlemen.—Our client, Mr John Pemberton, contra tor,who is a member of the Stockton Heath Parish Council, has consulted us with regard to the procerdings at a meeting of that Council held on the 2nd May last. It was propo4ed by Mr George Pilling (district councillor for Latchford, and not a ratepayer in Stockton Heath) and seconded by Mr Joseph Knowles (district councillor for Appleton, and not as ratepayer in StoActon Reath Parish) that the sum of £lO be given to the District Surveyor for the Runcorn District Council out of the special rare for his extra services Besides the proposer and seconder,who are not ratepayers of Stock-on Heath. Mr Pearson, who is not a ratepayer in Stockton Heath, and Mr Whitley, who is a rate- payer, voted in favour of the proposal. Toe proposal was opposed by Mr Joseph Clarke, Mr J iho Pemberton, and Mr George Mason.all members of the Parish Couacil and ratepayers in Stockton Heath, The Surveyor is appointed by. the Runco-n Roral District Counll for one half of its district of which Stockton Heatn forms a small p set. Be is paid a salary by the Runcorn District Council which receives and distributes the increase in the rates at Stocktoo Heath for all new assessments. The special rate referred to is one t tat ' was levied some veers ago for the purpose of laying the main :sewers and there has since been added to t the emptying of ashpits and the gas lighting. Toe sewers were laid about 6ix years ago, and the emptying cf ashpits and gas lighting is not included in the duties of the district surveyor, in fact he has performed no services that can be p:op'.rly charged on this special fund. If the surveyor has rendered arty extra services he should not be remunerated out of this special rate, hut the Runeora Rural District Council which receives the benefit of all increased and new assessments in Stockton Heath should raise the salary of its surveyor out of the I genera! rates, otherwise as is ebvious Stockton Heath would be paying the £lO extra to the surveyor out of its special rate, while all the increased rates would he received and distributed generally by the Runcorn Rural 'District Council. The proposal of the Parochial C ,rn- , mittee requires your board's consent, and after this explanation and considering that there was only one Stockton Heath ratepayer in favour of the proves!, whilst three voted against it, we hope your board will not reel justified is giving yoor consent. We are, your obedient servants, Spencer Wellhead and Son. S. B. Provis, Esq., secretary Local Government Board, Whitehall, S.W.

The Cleili:ha.ving read the above, said that the n ,iy reply they could send would be the resolution passed by the District Council, spine time previously, that If the Surveyor did attend such mnetingq. the expenses must be piid by a special rate chargeable on the special Dis- trict.

Mr Linaker licked whether ti awning of the kind appertained to Frodshatn. The Clerk replied that about two years ac', they passed a resolution to the effect that the surveyors should be p tid out of a special rate, and that had been sanc- tioned. Rut that year's account for Frodshatn had not been .?anctioned.

Toe Cnairnaan (Mr owles) pointed out that he had voted on the questios conscientiously. (Hear. bear). The surveyor was doing work for the Parish Council, when he might be employed elsewhere ; and besides Frodsbam and:Balton, as well as Appleton wereloblized to nay. Mr Woodward then proposed that the District confirm by vote, that afternoon, what had already been done in the matter. (Hear. hear). There was an in- crease in the surveyor's salary. It was simply a remuneration to Mr Swinton for work that the Stockton Beath Committee specially required, and which in all probability the District Council would never have required him to do. (Hear, hear). Mr Linaker seconded, and the motion was unani- mously carried.

COUNCIL.
The School Board Campaign.
Lecture on the Educa'ion Questions by Mr. Hirst Hollowell.

IThe Runcorn Free Church Council conducted the first of a series of meetings to be held in connection with the forth- coming School Board Election, at the Bethesda Lecture Hall, Runcorn. on Tuesday evening last. The chair was taken 1)5, the Rev Alfred Wells (president of the Commit). On his right sat Mr Hirst Hollowell (secretary of the Northern Counties Education League). and supportiug him were :-Messrs S Taylor, F J Norman, J Pritchard, W Handley (members of the Runcorn School Board) ; the Revs J Osborne, if Morrison and J B Foster; Messrs J Wilson, A R Norman and others. The attendance was large, and inclu- ded a number of influential townspeople. The Chairman, who was cordially received, said Sir John Brunner had promised to be present, but he (the chairman) had to say he was unable to be ~,on account of being kept in London by an important Committee of the House of Commons, that it was very imperative he should attend. (Hear, hear). When he said It was a cemmittee which dealt with the Education question, they would agree with him that Sir John would be more able to serve their cause by his presence there, th at by his presence in that hall. (Loud epplause). The question of Education was tee one they had met to consider, and he presumed they all believed in the importance cf it. (Ap- plause). As the mouthpiece of the Free Church Council he wished to say they fully believed in the education of the whale man ; in the education of the mind and heart : Intel cot and affections. They had the right to expect that the state would provide the means for the edueatlon of every child. As an Englishman ;as a private member of society. and none the less as a Nonconformist he objected to having to seed his child, u tde o the compulsion. of the law of the land, to any school except whore hls child would be taught what he considered it ought to be taught. (Loud applause.) He positively objected to send his child to any denominational school which was not in harmony with his wishes. (Hear, hear.) He ought no more to be compelled to send a boy of his to a Church of England school, simply because there wore no vacancies in the Board Scholl. than a Church of Ragland cleloiman ought to be obliged to send his boy to a Wesleyan School for the same reason. (Loud applause.) Let the ahurches of the land look after the religious training ; and let them require the state to provide ample accommodation for every child it requiret to be eduoated. (Hear, hear and applause., The Rev J Os`aerne then read the following resolution :- " That this meeting rejoices at (the abandonment of the Education Bill. but protests against the attempt to carry into law by means of a smaller measure. those clauses of the Bill, which would subject School Boards in respect to their Higher Grade and evening continuation soh ools. to the Interference and veto of County Committees that have not been elected for Elucationel purposes. Farther that this meeting regards with alarm the unfair influence which cleric- alism is exereising on our educational policy. It deplores the great injustice which results to Nonconformists, and prays the Government in any proposed change, to ensure that :-( t). All the elementary schools in the land which receive grants (coin the public purse should be open to all duly qualified teachers, without any reeerd to the religious denomination to which they belong. (2). That no public money should be granted for elementary education without its expenditure being under an eff eetive controlling author- ity, directly and expressly elected by the ratepayers for that purpose. (3). That as an act of justice to all parents and children, an unsectarian school, under effective public control, should be established within reasonable distance of every child, and that the School Board area should be sufficiently large to secure independence and efficiency. (4) That no educational disa- bility whatsoever should atta oh to any child on mum unt of the religion of its parents, and that the imposition of any religious test shculd be stoutly resisted. (5) That adequate provision should be made in National Colleges to train and admit to the teaching profession capable persons on equal terms, whatever may be the religious denomination to which they may be attached. (6) That tea :hers in public elemen- tary schools shall not be required to do extraneous work as a condition of their employment as teachers." (Loud applause.) The Chairman then moved the proposition, which was most enthusiastically r-ceived, and called upon The ifev. J. Hirst Hollowell, who sec ailed the re notation and said the absence of Sir John Brunner was his loss as much as theirs. They could all welcome Sir John Brunner's presence as a man and as an educationist, for if ever there was an educationist In Parliament. Sir John was one both in spirit and in action. Now while that night they were to speak of a national question of the greatest gravity, and the fact that this meeting was held under the auspices of the Free, or to use their historic name, the Nonconformiet Churches accounted for the other fact that it was national policy they were there to advocate. (Hear. hear.) Nonconformists in education had only one policy and that was a national policy. (Hear. hear.) They did not wish that any Nonconformist Shibboleth or creed or polity should be taught in day schools at the public expense. (Hear, hear) As Nonconformists they repudiated sectarian Nonconformity taught in schools that were filled by compulsion. When people said this was a battle between church and chapel, they did not know what they were talking about. Noncon- formists came to the front in educational battles not because they wanted Nonconformist day schools but because their policy was a national policy. (Applause ) The education ' position in England and Wales was one that satisfied nobody. Even the Tory Government was constantly twinging in Education Bills and haying to take them out again. (Laur.ter). Although the late defunct and not lamented Education Bill had been withdrawn, he must warn them that If possible the Government would bring the very worst elements In a small measure, which they thought they could drive through the House by the unscrupulous use if the closure. That remained to be seen. 'lt Was intended to take the Bth and 9th clauses, which subordinated and humiliated and displaced and degraded School Boards, forced the School Board of London. elected tss five millions of peeple, to go cap in hind to a Comity , Committee that had not been chosen for education at all. (Shame.) The Governme it were col, gto try in that way to destroy the higher e iucation of the industrial classes. The industrial claises ought to destroy them. (Hear, hear.) Of course his accent politically. (Laughter.) Last year he formed one of a deputation to the Duke of Devonshire on education questions and the Duke replied that"lt is obviously impossibleifor the present Government and the members of th present Parliament to make any change in the law. It is almost a waste of time to go to a member of the present" government ant ask him to propose any radical alteration in the legal.status cf education." This was not‘a very flattering account of the last Government or of the last parliament. A. waste of time to ask for reform from the last Parliament 1 Some of then-, thought the present Parliament not any better. What was the legal status of education in this country. We had not a single training college that was , under the control of the state, (Shaine ) Talk abort the , Voluntary system in this country, they had not got a vol- untary system like the United States. Where they had a I graded system, under a single authority, controlled in all its grades by the elect of the people, it was there they had a grand development of Voluntaryism. They could never have true Voluntaryism until they had a true perfect State system' In California one lady and gentleman between them gave three million pounds sterling to found a university that shonld be open to every lad and girl in the state. (Applause.) People would lay the top stone on a good system but a wretched mongrel system such aa they had in England, they could not expect to elicit any enthusiasm. (Hear, hear.) That was i one part of the legal status of education. There were 43 training c illeges and all hut eight were In sectarian hands. (Shame.) It was almost impossible to let young people be trainedlas teachers unless they profesee !attachment to one or other forms of Churchrnanship. Young people were barred out of training colleges in this free country by religious tests. This was part of the legal status of education that he wished to see altered. If they had three hundred Sir John Brunner's in the House of Commons Englsed would not be two years older without seeing some state training colleges like those they hal in Mass. U.S.A. The legal status of education in England was of this curious sort, that as long as volunteers would cover the ground with schools of almost any quality, however ramshackle-as bog as railway com- panies, jumble sales, voluntary rates, and begging clergymen would join to build enough schools to hold the bodies of the children, however sectarian the schools might be. the people had no right to have a Board School. This was infamy, What would they say on Sunday morning on walking out to and in Runcorn no house of prayer except Church of England and the law compelled every person to worship there? There were 8 000 places where children walked to every morning and found only a Charch of England day school and the law said "to that school you must go." There were 160 of these places in the fertile, but not very progressive County of Cheshire -(laughter)-160 villages and small towns In Cheshire where there was absolutely no school but Anglican or Roman Catho:ic, and still it was a free country. Some of the counties like Lancashire and Somersetshire had three hundred such places. As long as any rrivate people would un tertake the job and provide a sufficient Number of school places to hold the helpless bodies of the infants, then liberty was dead : the community had absolutely no tight to have schools under municipal control. This was a state of the law they ought to be ashamed of, and if the Liberals were worth their salt-and there was a good deal of salt in this country,-(laughter)-they ought to rise up and alter thia state of thing. (Applause). Then they had the Conscience Clause. They knew what the , working mate said when told "You will have to I Send the child CO the Priest's school, but never ' mind there will be the Conscience Clause," he I replied with greater humour than grammatical correctness • . I ain't a going to put My clailds' conscience in anybody's claws." (Laughter.) His spelling was wrong but hie mean- ing was right. (Laughter ) The speaker described the perse- cution that arose from the operation of the ODOCIICiO`ICO clause. Clergymen and managers of Volnutary Schools told them that they could do what they liked because the schools were their schools, the teachers were their teachers and the playgrounds were their playgrounds and that they paid money which kept up the schools. Ile chal- lenged that claim. (Applause ) Many of those schools were nit even built by the people who control them. Public money was voted towards the bricks and morter sad the furof,hing of the schools. (Applause.) There were scores of such schools in Cheshire. The child was compelled to attend. the taxpayer compelled to Day, and the teacher, earning a livelihood in a gallant and noble profession was compelled to conform and this was what was called voluntaryism. Dealing with the Cockerton judgment, Mr Hollowell described it as a deliberate attempt, in which the Prime Minister and kis two sons and his nephew had tagen a prominent part to crush out the higher grade schools and evening continuation schools throughout the length and breadth of the land. It was a int ohievaus thinz, which upset the best work of the past thirty years, a period which bad been the brightest and best in the annals of the nation's history. The Clo-kertga Judgment WAS the ore thing, in his opinion, which would meet with the derision of history and posterity. (Hear, hear.) If they wanted to know what had killed the Government Education Bill, it was the Cockerton judgment that killed it. (Applause.) And no Government that brought about anything like a Cockerton judgment omeht to be entrusted with the passing of an Educational Bill. (Ilear,hear.) They were not At tor the work They in Runcorn would be asked to pronounce .heir verdict in the matter shortly, and he hoped when the time came, they would unmistakably pronounce that the e lucation of their country, should at any rate be as perfect as that of any other nation in the world. (Loud and prolonged applause.) Mr. James Pritchard. Mr W. Handley and the Chairman further supported the motion, which was subsequently carried unanimously, and copies of the resolution were directed to be forwarded to Sir John Gorst and the Duke of Devonshire. and to Sir J T Brunner.
Votes of thanks t) the leclurer and chalrman concluded a most enthuliastie meeting,

div.head: "A GIRL OF THE PEOPLE,"
div.p: "A GIRL OF THE PEOPLE,"
BY MRS. 0. N. WILLIAMSON.

diTETCEI OF THE STORY. Miss. Wililitimiox's ideal of a story for serial Publication is that it should have In It something or excitement. of suspense, of mystery, and even of horror,and these characteristics will certainly Se found in " A Girl of the People." The heroine of the *Pony. Sheila Cope, finds herself suddenly by the singular occurrences on the occasion of a visit to a theatre with her supposed mother Lady Cope, plunged in the mi,lst of a series of mysterious happenings. The mystery concerns herself, her mother, and a woman she had seen in the stalls, and It is one which Is not solved for many a day. for Lady Cope, before any explanation c-n be given. dies suddenly of the shock and horror of the thing. Sheila then finds she was the adopted daughter of Lady Cope, and that her mother is a poor woman living in a squalid street in Peckarn. Sir Roger Cope, a nephew of the dead lady, announces that no will was left, and that he i• Lady Cope's heir.but he offers to marry Sheila, who, however, feels an in- vincible avarsion to him, and Roos hurriedly to her mother's hose. Ryan here, she Is not free from the persecutions of Sir Roger Cope and his agelits. Ail her attempts to get work are thwarl.ed, her money. and her jewellery, on which she had hoped to raise enough to live for some time. are stolen, and in her desperate plight there seems to be no resource for her but a leap from Waterloo Bridge into the darkly flowing Thames. A good friend comes to the rescue just in time in one John Bourke, a Labour V.P.,who proves the best of good Samaritans,and between him and his pro.egea a very tender feeling of regard and affection springs up. Even from this haven. however, Shelia is forced to fly, and many are the adventures she has to pass through, till the mystery of Lady Cope's death Is cleared up, mad a way made for h.r happiness and that of Bourke. It is a story not only of great sensational interest, but one in which passages of rare charm abound.

STOCKTON H EATH. MEETING OF THE PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE. A meeting of the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee was held in the National Schoolroom, Stockton Heath, on Thursday last week. In the absence of Mr Davenport through illness, the chair was taken by Mr Clarke. There were also present :—Messrs Fairhurst, Whitley, Pilling,Pemberton,Mclntyre, with G F Ashton(clerk), J winton (surveyor), and J Farrington (nuisance inspec- tor). PLANS —A BUILDER ORDERED TO STOP BUILDING Mr Swinton read the correspondence he bad had with Mr Mather respecting the houses that gentleman pro- posed to erect on the Pike estate. The plans were dis- approved because Mr Mather did not submit the plans on the required tracing paper and did hot show the re. quired levels. Mr s winton submitted plans of houses being erect el by Mr Twigs. On the proposition of Mr Pemberton, tins, c@mmittee decided that Mr Twise be called upon to stop building on the back passage of Dundonald Avenue. It was stated that Mr Tcsiis had commenced building before the plans were submitted to the committee. NEW BYELAWS. The Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board confirming the byelaws of the committee relative to privies and ashpits. A further communication was read from the Board stating that they would proceed to issue an order putting into force the section of the Towns Improvement Clauses Act, in Stockton Heath dealing with water from roofs. THE INCREASE 05' ma. SWINTON'S SALARY. The Local Government Board submitted for the ob- servation of the Rural Council, copies of correspondence they bad received from Mr Joseph Clarke of Heathfield, Stockton Heath, and Messrs Wallhead ar.d Son, on II?. half of Mr John Pemberton' referring to the fact that the resolution granting RIO additional salary to Mr Swinton, surveyor, and chargeable to Stockton Heath was passed by rural councillors coming from adjoining districts and that only one representative of Stockton Heath voted for the proposition. The Clerk stated that the correspondence would be considered by the Rural Council at the meeting on Tuesday next. A DESIRABLE IMPROVEMENT. Mr Reginald Potts, clerk to the Cheshire Ciunty Coun- cil, wrote with reference to the footpath at the end of Chapel-lane and Walton-road, pointing out that he cost of construction had been included in the estimates of the Council for the current year, and that being so, the work would be put in hand very shortly. TIIE PROPOSED SLAITGEITER HOUSE. A PETITION AGAINST IT. The Clerk read a petition signed by 35 residents in Gaskell-street and neighbourhood praying the com- mittee to rescind the resolution granting a licence for the erection of a slaughter house at the rear of G •skell- street on the ground mainly, that it would be a danger to children. The clerk pointed out that the licence had been granted by the Rural D.strict Council on the recommendation of the Parochial Committee. It was decided that the Clerk should write to the memorialists stating that the licence for the erection of the slaughter house had been granted, but that the matters referred to in the petition had been considered by the Committee and steps would be taken to avoid the danger complained of. This was all the business of public interest.
